## 11.9 Complexification of Lie algebras

It was seen that a real vector space can become a complex vector space by complexification. Indeed, the carrier set for the sort SCALAR was swapped from the real numbers to the complex numbers. Correspondingly, the complex field was utilized in place of the real number field. Concurrently, carrier sets for the sort VECTOR were adjusted to include imaginary parts. Operators from the signature sets with names S-MULT and V-ADD were used in mapping the new elements in accordance with their definitions. In short, scalar multiplication and vector addition are closed using complex manipulations. Since the tangent space is a vector space, the vector space complexification is applicable. Similar to a Hilbert space situation, the tensor product Hc=Hr ⊗![Equation](Images/F000126si53.png) C is applicable.

For a Lie algebra, the Lie bracket must also be complexified. In this case, for A, B, D, and E in the Lie algebra g, then the complexification of the Lie bracket is given by a form similar to the polarization identity: \[A + i B, D + i E\]=\[A, D\]−\[B, E\] + i\[A, E\] + i\[B, D\] ([Humphreys, 1997](#Ch011_191-216_B9780443136979000126.xhtml#bib10)). Finally, realize that the matrix A + Bi is shorthand for A⊗1 + B⊗i, where ⊗![Equation](Images/F000126si54.png) is the tensor product. As a result, complexification is similar to just complexification of a vector space. An excellent example follows using a Lie algebra, which is falsely assumed to be a complex algebra.

 

### Example 11.31

The Lie algebra su(n, C) is the algebra with Lie bracket being the commutator consisting of all matrices M, such that M\*=−M. These matrices are skew Hermitian, or skew symmetric and with a trace of M equaling zero. Note that this Lie algebra is not complex; it is real, because as a vector space it is real. This follows using M, then (Mi)\*=−M\*i=Mi. Refer to the vector space definition. Here, the SCALAR sort determines whether the vector space is real or complex. In any case, the most general matrix in su(2, C) is M=

$\\begin{array}{ll} {|{ix}} & {{- c \\ast}|} \\\\ {|c} & {{ - {ix}}|} \\\\ \\end{array}$

![Equation](Images/F000126si55.png)

where x is real and c is a complex number. A basis for this Lie algebra is given next, and they are related to the Pauli matrices, sj, j=1, 2, and 3. Given below in order are M1=is1, M2=−is2, and M3=is3. These are also denoted X, Y, and Z:

$\\begin{array}{llllll} {|0} & { i|} & {|0} & {{- 1}|} & {|i} & {\\quad 0|} \\\\ {|i} & {0|} & {|1} & {\\mspace{20mu} 0|} & {|0} & {{- i}|} \\\\ \\end{array}$

![Equation](Images/F000126si56.png)

The commutators \[M1, M2\]=2 M3, \[M2, M3\]=2 M1, and finally, \[M3, M1\]=2 M2. \[Mi, Mj\]=2 Eijk Mk. Here, the Levi-Civita symbol Eijk is once again employed. The Lie algebra sl(2,C)=su(2,C) + su(2,C) i. This expression will provide the complexification of su(2,C). The most general element in the special linear algebra, sl(2,C), is N=

$\\begin{matrix} {|{x + {iy}}} & {{\\mspace{22mu} u + {iv}}|} \\\\ {|{r + {is}}} & {{- x - {iy}}|} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000126si57.png)

This matrix has complex values, and the trace equals zero. A basis for this Lie algebra is given in the order, N1, N2, and N3 as follows:

$\\begin{array}{rrrrrr} {|1} & {0|} & {|0} & {1|} & {|0} & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & {{- 1}|} & {|0} & {0|} & {|1} & {0|} \\\\ \\end{array}$

![Equation](Images/F000126si58.png)

Going back to su(2, C) and now utilizing the above basis shows that the most general matrix in su(2, C) is M=ixN1−c\*N2 + cN3, since M is given by:

$\\begin{matrix} {|{ix}} & {{- c \\ast}|} \\\\ {|c} & {{ - {ix}}|} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000126si59.png)

This is not surprising since su(2,C) is a sub-Lie algebra of sl(n, C). The objective is to see the expansion involving the complexification of su(2, C). Now consider the most general matrix in sl(2, C), which is N=−ixM3 + yM3−u/2 (M2 + i M1)−iv/2 (M2 + i M1) + r/2 (M2−iM1) + is/2 (M2−iM1). This shows that the two Lie algebras are essentially the same. Moreover, note that only six complexified basis elements of su(2, C) are needed in describing N. These six matrices are M1, M2, M3, iM1, iM2, and iM3. Again, this is expected since the dimension of sl(2, C) is six over the real field.#

 Chapter 13 

# Spectra for operators

 

## Abstract

The criteria for showing the existence of a spectrum are reviewed. Spectral applications are provided of the Lumer-Phillips theorem for adjoint operators and dual operators in Banach space. Descriptions, as well as examples, are given for the point spectrum, the continuous spectrum, along with the residual spectrum in both Banach and Hilbert spaces. The Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem is stated and illustrated for unbounded operators, including the momentum and distance operators. The numerical range is described in reference to spectral values along with dissipative and accretive operators. Conditions for which symmetric operators are self-adjoint are provided. The approximate eigenvalue concept is described along with applications to compact operators. The Cauchy integral theorem is utilized for determining the resolvent set. The chapter ends with an introduction to spectral measures and spectral theory. Additionally, in the last section, an example of Stieltjes integration is illustrated. Also, projective-valued measures are described in reference to the spectral theorems.

 

### Keywords

Lumer-Phillips theorem; Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem; one-parameter semigroups; dissipative operator; accretive operator; Stieltjes integral; residual spectrum; approximate spectrum; saltus

 

## 13.1 Spectral classification for bounded operators

This section is a continuation of [Sections 8.5](#Ch008_145-164_B9780443136979000059.xhtml#s0030) and [8.6](#Ch008_145-164_B9780443136979000059.xhtml#s0035). The principal references for a major earlier part of this chapter are [Halmos (1957)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib20) and [He’lein (2014)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib21). In [Chapter 8](#Ch008_145-164_B9780443136979000059.xhtml#Ch008_145-164_B9780443136979000059), the criteria originating with the first reference ([Halmos, 1957](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib20)) were provided for illustrating the existence of a spectrum, specifically, the spectrum spT in Hilbert space H. The necessary and sufficient condition is repeated here. For an operator T, in B(H,H), spT={c, such that c in C, and (c I−T) is not invertible iff both 1) and 2) hold}:

1.  1) The image of T is dense in H, and
2.  2) There is a scalar, a> 0 such that for all v in H‖Tv‖>a‖v‖.

In the second reference given earlier, criterion (1) is referred to as weakly onto, and the second criterion number (2) is implied to be strongly one to one.

For T, in B(H,H), it was previously shown that the spectrum of T is nonempty and forms a compact set in C. Moreover, the resolvent set, RsT, is an open set in C. This set *R**s**T* = {*λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si3.png), where *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si4.png) is in C, and such that (T−*λ*I) is one to one and onto, (*T*−*λ**I*)^( − 1)![Equation](Images/F000138si5.png) is bounded}. The boundedness of the inverse follows also from the bounded inverse theorem. This theorem can be found in Appendix A.6. Additionally, a partition of the spT is provided by three disjoint sets sppT, spcT, and sprT. Briefly, the spectra will be described for T, a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, X differing from {0}. The inner product is not necessary for this development; thus a Banach space is utilized. Numorous examples are provided, and in the unbounded case they are presented in a formal manner. Domain issues are not considered.

1.  1) The point spectrum sppT={*λ* in C such that (T−*λ*I) is not one to one on X}.
2.  2) The continuous spectrum spcT={*λ* in C such that (T−*λ*I) is one to one on X, but it is not onto X; however, it has ran (T−*λ*I) dense in X}.
3.  3) The residual spectrum sprt={*λ* in C such that (T−*λ*I) is one to one and not onto, but with ran (T−*λ*I) not dense in X}.

 

1.  1) For sppT, Ker(*λ* I−T) is not {0}; there must exist a nonzero vector f in X such that T f=*λ* f, f→(T−*λ*I)f. This mapping is not one to one in X; any nonzero multiple of f satisfies this criterion, since any nonzero scalar times an eigenvector is again an eigenvector. In complex n-dimensional space, dim (Ran (T))+dim (Ker (T))=n. Additionally, f in X is called an eigenvector, and *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si6.png) is called an eigenvalue. In finite-dimensional Hilbert space, there only exists this point spectrum. Several examples of the point spectrum have been illustrated using matrix operations in finite-dimensional Banach or Hilbert space. A most trivial illustration of the point spectrum in an infinite-dimensional space is given in Example 8.16. Additional examples in infinite-dimensional Hilbert space with a point spectrum are provided in [Examples 13.1](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun1) and [13.2](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun2).
2.  2) For spcT, Ker(*λ* I−T) is {0}, and the image of *λ*I−T is dense in H, but Im (*λ* I−T) is not equal to X. Equivalently, *λ*I−T is dense in H iff ker (*λ*I−T)∗={0}. Since Ker(*λ* I−T) is {0}, (*λ* I−T) (f[1] – f[2])=0; this implies that f[1]\=f[2], so (T−*λ*I) is one to one on X. It is not onto because if it were then Im (*λ* I−T)=X. Instances of this spectrum are given in Examples 8.17 and 8.18.
3.  3) Ker(*λ* I−T) is {0}, the image of *λ*I−T is not dense in H, and Im (*λ* I−T) is not equal to H; then *λ* is in the residual spectrum. This means that the operator T having a residual spectrum is far away from being onto. The associated spectrum is denoted by sprT. An example of a nonempty residual spectrum is provided in [Example 13.3](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun3) ([Stack Exchange, 2016](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib13)).

 

### Example 13.1

Consider, l^(*p*), for p in \[1, ∞), with scalars in C. For *λ*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si7.png), *λ*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si8.png), *λ*[3]![Equation](Images/F000138si9.png), … in C and bounded, that is, sup|*λ*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si10.png)|<∞. Let T be an infinite scalar matrix T: l^(*p*)→l^(*p*), with T having values of *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si11.png) in order on the main diagonal. Using the standard basis implies that Tv[*n*]\=*λ*[*n*]v[*n*] where the eigenvector is v[*n*]\=(0 0 … 0 1 0…), and the 1 is in the nth tuple position. So sppT is a subset of the set spT. That is, v[*n*] are eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues *λ*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si12.png).

In the closure of the set of all eigenvalues, there could exist a point c in C, and this point is in the spectrum. If there exists a limit point c, for the set of all *λ*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si13.png), then c cannot be in sppT, but c is in spT. This will happen in the closure of the set of all eigenvalues. For instance, if *λ*[*n*]\=1/n, then 0 would be in the spectrum of T, that is, it is sprT or spcT.#

 

### Example 13.2

Let T: l²→l² over the complex field. For any v in l², we have that T(v1, v2, v3, …)=(v1, v2/2, v3/3, …). The point spectrum is {1, 1/2, 1/3, …}. This can easily be seen by writing an infinite scalar matrix with values 1/n on the main diagonal. Using the standard basis implies that Tv[*n*]\=*λ*[*n*]v[*n*] where the eigenvector is v[*n*]\=(0 0 … 0 1 0…), and the value one is in the nth tuple position. So sppT is a subset of the set spT. That is, v[*n*] are eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues *λ*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si14.png). The value zero is a limit point of eigenvalues. So zero would also be spT.#

 

### Example 13.3

This is an example of the residual spectrum being nonempty. Let the carrier set for the Hilbert space H be l², the space of all square absolute summable sequences with complex entries. For T: l²→l², consider T(v1, v2, v3, …)=(0, v1, v2/2, v3/3, …). This is a right-shift operation. The Ker( c I - T ) ={0}. T v1=0, T v2=v1, T v3=v2/2 …. So again, the spectrum is not empty, and zero is a spectral point, because of the noninvertible criteria. T is not onto, since the first tuple in the codomain is fixed. If vn is a unit vector with 1 at position n and 0 elsewhere, then Tvn---> 0. See [Stack Exchange (2016)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib13). Note that the dual operator T∗ is such that <T∗w, v>=<w, Tv>. Since T(v1, v2, v3, …)=(0, v1, v2/2, v3/3, …), substituting into the leftmost inner product gives w1′∗v1+w2′∗v2+w3′∗v3 +…=w1· Next expanding the other inner product results in 0+w2 v1+w3 v2/2 +…. Here, wj′∗=T∗wj. Next, equating coefficients of vj implies that w1′∗=w2, w2′∗=w3/2, …. Therefore, T∗ (w1, w2, w3, …)=(w2, w3/2, …). It is a left-shift type operation.#

 

## 13.2 Spectra for operators on a Banach space

The spectrum of the adjoint operators when they exist is often related to the spectrum of the original operator. The Lumer-Phillips theorem is a useful tool for determining the spectrum of adjoint operators in Hilbert and Banach spaces ([Lumer and Philips, 1961](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib9)). This theorem was used in [He’lein (2014)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib21), to illustrate the distinct types of spectra for bounded operators in a Banach space. Many of these same examples are repeated in the following section. First, however, Lumer-Phillips theorem specifies that, in a Banach space A with T′ being the dual operator of T in A, the spectra spT=spT′. Moreover, for c in the resolvent set Rs(T), the resolvent operators Rc(T)′=Rc(T′). Also, for T in a Hilbert space with adjoint T∗, it follows that spT∗=(spT)∗={c∗|c in the spectrum of T, that is, c in spT}. Finally, for c in the resolvent set Rs(T), the resolvent operators: Rc∗(T∗)=(Rc(T))∗.

The Banach space l¹ has a dual space l^∞; additionally, there is a continuous isomorphism from l^∞ into the dual space of l¹. Consider a continuous linear operator *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si15.png), *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si16.png): l^∞→C. Let en, n=0, 1, 2, …, in l¹ be a basis where en=(0, 0, …0, 1, 0, …) and has one in the nth tuple and zero elsewhere. For v in l¹, where v=(v0, v1, v2, …), the norm of the difference $\\left\\| {v - \\sum\_{n = 0}^{N}\\left( {{vn} \\cdot {en}} \\right)} \\right\\|$![Equation](Images/F000138si17.png) is less than or equal to $\\sum\_{N + 1}^{\\infty}\\left| {vn} \\right|$![Equation](Images/F000138si18.png), which goes to zero as N goes to infinity, since vn is absolute summable. Now using *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si19.png) and then employing the continuity condition gives $\\phi\\left( v \\right) = \\lim\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}\\phi\\left. \\lbrack{\\sum\_{n = 0}^{N}\\left( {{vn} \\cdot {en}} \\right)} \\right\\rbrack = \\lim\_{N\\rightarrow\\infty}\\sum\_{n = 0}^{N}{\\left( {{vn} \\cdot \\phi\\left\\lbrack {en} \\right\\rbrack} \\right) =}\\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}\\left( {{vn} \\cdot \\phi\\left\\lbrack {en} \\right\\rbrack} \\right)$![Equation](Images/F000138si20.png). Since *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si21.png) is continuous for all w in l¹ and since *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si22.png) is bounded, ‖*ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si23.png)‖ is less than or equal to c, where c> 0. Also,|*ϕ*(w)|is less than or equal to ‖*ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si24.png)‖ ‖w‖. In particular,|*ϕ*(en)|is less than or equal to ‖*ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000138si25.png)‖ ‖en‖=c. So *ϕ*(en) is bounded, and as a consequence, the series for $\\phi\\left( v \\right) = \\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}\\left( {{vn} \\cdot \\phi\\left\\lbrack {en} \\right\\rbrack} \\right)$![Equation](Images/F000138si26.png) is absolutely converging; $\\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}\\left| {{vn} \\cdot \\phi\\left\\lbrack {en} \\right\\rbrack} \\right|$![Equation](Images/F000138si27.png) is less than or equal to c $\\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}\\left| {vn} \\right|$![Equation](Images/F000138si28.png). It follows that ∥*ϕ*∥![Equation](Images/F000138si29.png) is less than ∥*ϕ*(*e**n*)∥![Equation](Images/F000138si30.png) because a bounded operator norm is the infimum of the Lipschitz constant M, where ∥*ϕ*(*v*)∥![Equation](Images/F000138si31.png) is less than or equal to M‖v‖. This implies that ∥*ϕ*∥ = ∥*ϕ*(*e**n*)∥![Equation](Images/F000138si32.png).

Several examples that follow ([He’lein, 2014](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib21)) involve the Banach space l¹ and its dual space l^∞. In the following, the range and image of an operator T are used interchangeably. That is, ranT=imT; they are the same. Additionally, the closure of an operator is denoted by closT.

 

### Example 13.4

Consider the Banach space l¹ of all complex-valued sequences v=(v1, v2, …), which are absolutely summable. Let L be the left-shift operator L (v)=(v2, v3, …). The dual operator is denoted by L∗ and not symbolized as L′ for readability purposes. It operates in the dual space I^∞, the space of bounded sequences w=(w1, w2, …). Even though the inner product is not applicable, it will be employed as an operational calculus device to quickly find the adjoint. So formally, taking the inner product <w, L (v)>=w1∗v2+w2∗v3+…. Next, to find L∗, use <L∗ (w), v> and then equate this result to the sum written earlier as <L∗ (w), v>=w1′∗v1+w2′∗v2+w3′∗v3+…, where the prime, that is, wn′∗, indicates the nth tuple of L∗(w). Equating coefficients of vk involving <L∗ (w), v> and <w, L (v)>, and solving for wk′∗, gives w1′∗=0, w2′∗=w1∗, w3′∗=w2∗, …. This shows that the dual operator L∗ (w)=(0, w1, w2, …). The resulting operation is the right shift.

Note that ∥*L*^(*n*)∥ = ∥(*L*\*)^(*n*)∥ = 1![Equation](Images/F000138si33.png), and the norm equals the spectral radius for both L and L∗. Gelfand’s formula from [Section 8.10](#Ch008_145-164_B9780443136979000059.xhtml#s0055), shows this. Here the limit n→∞, of ∥*L*^(*n*)∥^(1/*n*)\=*r*(*L*)=1=*l**i**m**i**t* *n*→∞![Equation](Images/F000138si34.png), of ∥(*L*\*)^(*n*)∥^(1/*n*) = *r*(*L*\*) = 1![Equation](Images/F000138si35.png). Because of this result, the spectra of L and L∗ lie in the closure of an open ball centered at the origin, and of radius one. The ball is denoted clos(O(0,1)). Where clos represents the closure operation. All the points of the open ball are eigenvalues, that is, O(0,1) is a subset of sppL. If v=(1, 0, 0, …), then v is an eigenvector of L with c=0 as an eigenvalue, because L(v)=0 v. Other points c in O(0,1) are also in sppL. To see this, let *v* = (1,*c*,*c*²,…)![Equation](Images/F000138si36.png) then *L*(*v*) = (*c*,*c*²,*c*³,…) = *c*(1,*c*,…) = *c* *v*![Equation](Images/F000138si37.png). Accordingly, the results mentioned earlier show that the open unit ball consists of eigenvalues for L.#

 

### Example 13.5

Again consider the Banach space l¹, as in [Example 13.4](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun4). This space consists of all complex-valued sequences v=(x1, x2, …), which are absolutely summable with L the left-shift operator L (v)=(x2, x3, …). It was seen in that example that the dual operator L∗ operates in the dual space *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si38.png), the space of bounded sequences w=(y1, y2, …). Moreover, the dual operator L∗ (w)=(0, y1, y2, …) is the right-shift operator. It was seen that the spectra of L and L∗ lie in the closure of an open ball centered at the origin with radius one, clos(O(0,1)). The inclusions hold: O(0,1) is contained in sppL, which itself is contained in spL, and this is contained in clos(O(0,1)). Then, since spL is compact, spL=clos(O(0,1))=spL∗, by the Lume-Phillips theorem. In [Example 13.4](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun4), it is shown that O(0,1) is a subset of sppL. Ultimately, it will be seen that O(0,1)=sppL, that is, the open unit ball is the point spectrum for L.

First note that the boundary of O(0,1) is not in sppL. That is, the boundary points are not eigenvalues. The boundary consists of {c, such that|c|=1}. Say that c is in ker(c−L) and not equal to {0}. This is proof by contradiction. Let v=(x1, x2, …) and then (c−L) v=0. That is, (c x1, c x2, …)=(x2, x3, …). A result of this identity is a recursive set of equations. Specifically, the recursion must hold, x(n+1)=c xn, n=1, 2,…. Solving, by using backward substitution, gives *v* = *c* *x*1(1,*c*,*c*²,…)![Equation](Images/F000138si39.png). Since|c|=1, v is not in *I*¹![Equation](Images/F000138si40.png), unless x1 is zero. It follows that the boundary is not in sppL, and therefore, the whole point spectrum is sppL=O(0,1).

Next, it will be seen that the point spectrum of L∗ is empty. Again assume not, that is, there is a complex value c such that (c−L∗) w=0 for a vector w=(y1, y2, …) in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si41.png). That is (c y1, c y2, …)=(0, y1, y2, …); this also leads to a set of equations, namely: c y1=0, c yk=y(k-1), k=2, 3, …. When c=0, then w=0 and cannot be an eigenvector. Otherwise, when c is not zero, then from the equations mentioned earlier, y1=0, and then by recursion, yk=0 for all k=2, 3, …. This implies that w=0, and it cannot be an eigenvector. Thus, sppL∗ is empty, and all that is known so far is that for the adjoint; the closed ball centered at the origin is the spectrum of L.#

 

### Example 13.6

Refer to Examples 13.4 and 13.5. The right-shift operator L∗ operates in the dual space *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si42.png), where for w=(y1, y2, …), L∗ (w)=(0, y1, y2, …). It will be seen that the open ball O(0,1) is in sprL∗. For c or c∗ in O(0,1), let *v* = (1,*c*,*c*²,…)![Equation](Images/F000138si43.png), so v is in *l*¹![Equation](Images/F000138si44.png), and the same holds for a vector involving the conjugates of c. To be in the residual spectrum of L∗, all that needs to be shown is the following: ker (c∗ I−L∗) is {0}, and the image of c∗I−L∗ is not dense in H. These criteria uniquely classify sprL. Consider any vector w in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si45.png), and using again, only in a formal manner, a map of the form, f: w→<w, v>. Accordingly, f: (c∗−L∗) w→<(c∗−L∗) w, v>=<w, (c−L) v>=<w, c v−L v>. Use the definition of the operator L, and notice that c v−Lv=0, because all points c in the open ball are eigenvalues. This shows ker(c∗−L∗)={0}, and the image of c∗−L∗ is not dense, because for any w in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si46.png), f: (c∗−L∗) w=0; therefore, closf(c−L∗) cannot be dense in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si47.png). This shows that the open ball O(0,1) is in sprL∗.

Next, it will be shown that the residual spectrum of L∗ equals the closed unit ball, that is, sprL∗=clos(O(0,1)). Employ any complex number c, of unit length and vector u in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si48.png), and w in C. Use the vector tuples to form the set of equations resulting from the following identity: (c−L∗) w=u. Expanding the identity provides c w1=u1, and (c w2−w1)=u2,…, c wk−w(k-1)=uk, k=2, 3,…. Solving for vector w: w1=c∗u1, w2=c∗ (w1+u2),…, wk=c∗ (uk+w(k-1)). Back substitution gives the result: *w**k* = *c* \* *u**k* + *c*^( \* 2)*u*(*k* − 1) + … + *c*^( \* *k*)*u*1.*u* = (1, *c*\*,*c*^( \* 2), …)![Equation](Images/F000138si49.png) is in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si50.png), because the scalar c is of unit length and u is bounded. Substituting in the tuples of u into the expression for wk gives *w**k*\=*c*^( \* *n*)+*c*^( \* *n*)+…+*c*^( \* *n*)\=*k**c*^( \* *n*)→∞![Equation](Images/F000138si51.png) as *k*→∞![Equation](Images/F000138si52.png) and so the vector w is not in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si53.png). Thus, *u* = (1,*c*\*,*c*^( \* 2),…)![Equation](Images/F000138si54.png) is not in the image of (c−L∗). This shows that points on the boundary of the unit circle are not eigenvalues of L∗. So far, this shows that the boundary of the unit circle can be in the continuous or residual spectrum of L∗. Next, it will be shown that ran(cI−L∗) is not dense in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si55.png). Accordingly, these points will then be shown to be in the residual spectrum of L∗.

To see this, it will be shown that O (u, 1/2) intersects im(cI−L∗) and is empty in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si56.png). For v in O (u, 1/2), v=u+w, where the *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si57.png) norm,‖w‖is less than 1/2. Consider the equation: (cI−L∗) z=v=u+w. Here, z=(z1, z2, …) is a vector of complex-valued tuples, which is to be the solution of the aforementioned equation. It follows that *c* *z*1 − 0 = 1 + *w*1, *c* *z*2 − *z*1 = *c* \*  + *w*2, …, *c* *z**k* − *z*(*k*−1) = *c*^( \* *k* − 1) + *w**k*, *k* = 3, 4, ….![Equation](Images/F000138si58.png) Again, by substitution, solving tuple by tuple for the complex vector z yields ${zn} = c^{\\ast n} + \\sum\_{j = 1}^{n}\\left( {c^{\\ast n + 1 - j}{wj}} \\right)$![Equation](Images/F000138si59.png). Now using the bounds on c and the vector w shows that |*z**n* − *c*^( \* *n*)![Equation](Images/F000138si60.png)|is less than or equal to $|{\\sum\_{j = 1}^{n}\\left( {c^{\\ast n + 1 - j}{wj}} \\right)}|$![Equation](Images/F000138si61.png), which shows that |*z**n* − *c*^( \* *n*)| < *n*/2![Equation](Images/F000138si62.png). The vector zn is not bounded and therefore not in *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si63.png). This follows since |*z**n* − *c*^( \* *n*)![Equation](Images/F000138si64.png)|is greater or equal to |*c*^( \* *n*)| − |*z**n*| = *n* − |*z**n*|*o**r*|*z**n*|![Equation](Images/F000138si65.png) is greater than or equal to *n* − |*z**n* − *c*^( \* *n*)| > *n*/2![Equation](Images/F000138si66.png). This shows that the closure of (cI−L∗) is not *l*^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si67.png). Thus, sprL∗=|c|. Moreover, sprL∗ is the whole closed unit disk in C.#

 

### Example 13.7

For the left-shift operator L, in [Example 13.4](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun4), it will be seen that the residual spectrum is empty. Since it was shown in [Example 13.5](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun5) that O(0,1)=sppL, only the boundary of the unit ball need to be considered. So use a unit complex value c. That c is in sppL∗ is false since [Example 13.6](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun6) shows that sppL∗ is empty on the boundary|c|=1. The continuous spectra for L and L∗ are found using the fact that the three types of spectra are mutually disjoint and the union is the total spectra for each operator, which shows that spcL∗ is empty. Use the fact that sppL∗ is empty on|c|=1. Also, apply the proposition 6.3 (ii) from [He’lein, (2014)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib21). It states that if the ran (cI−L) is not dense in a Banach space, then c is in the sppL∗. From the contrapositive of this proposition, it follows that if sppL∗ is empty on |c|=1, then the ran (cI−L) is dense in *l*¹![Equation](Images/F000138si68.png); this implies that spcL equals the boundary of O(0,1). So, the boundary of the unit ball is the continuous spectrum of L.#

A summary of the results from [Examples 13.5](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun5)–[13.8](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun8) appears in [Fig. 13.1](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#f0010) ([He’lein, 2014](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib21)). In this figure, the closed unit disk appears twice, once to the left, for the left-shift operator L, and once for its dual operator L∗. The spectrum of L consists of a point spectrum sppL in the open unit disk in C. On the boundary of this disk is the continuous spectrum, spcL. The adjoint operator indicated on the right-hand side diagram shows that everywhere in the closed disk, L∗ has a residual spectrum, sprL∗.

## 13.3 Symmetric, self-adjoint, and unbounded operators

In quantum technology, the self-adjoint operator is of principal importance in that it is uniquely utilized in the observation process. This section and the next few sections are used in reviewing, extending, and illustrating numerous facts pertaining to self-adjoint operators both in the bounded and unbounded cases. Several illustrations of self-adjoint operators have been exhibited, mainly in terms of matrix operators. A simple example of a self-adjoint operator on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space follows.

 

### Example 13.8

This instance of a self-adjoint operator extends the results given in [Example 13.1](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#enun1). Let T: *l*²→*l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si69.png) over the complex field. For any v in *l*²,![Equation](Images/F000138si70.png) use the mapping, Tv=T(v1, v2, v3, …)=(v1, v2/2, v3/3, …). To be in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si71.png) means that the sum $\\sum\_{n = 1}^{\\infty}\\left( {vn} \\right)^{2}$![Equation](Images/F000138si72.png) converges. Consider w in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si73.png), where w=(w1, w2,…), and then the inner product <w, Tv>=w1∗v1+w2∗v2/ 2+w3∗v3/3+…. The definition of the adjoint operator involving the inner product is <T∗w, v>=w1′∗v1+w2′∗v2+w3′∗v3 +…. Here, wj′∗ is T∗wj. Then to see if there exists a relation between T and T∗, equate coefficients involving vn. This gives w1′∗=w1∗, w2∗′=w2∗/2, w3′∗=w3∗/3…. As a consequence, T∗w1=w1, T∗w2=w2/2, T∗w3=w3/ 3, …. Accordingly it follows that T∗=T, and so the operator T is self-adjoint.#

 

### Example 13.9

Let T: *l*²→*l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si74.png) over the complex field. For any v=(v0, v1, v2, v3, …), in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si75.png) say that Tv=(v1, v2/2, v3/3, …). To find T∗, notice that for w in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si76.png), <w, Tv>=w0∗v1+w1∗v2/2+…. Also forming <T∗w, v>=w0′∗v0+w1′∗ v1+…. Then equating the two inner product expressions together and then setting the coefficients of vn equal to each other yields: w0′∗=0, w1′∗=w0∗, w2′∗=w1∗/2, …. As a consequence, T∗w=(0, w0, w1/2, w2/3, …). So in this example T∗ does not equal T, so it is not self-adjoint. Notice, also that <T∗w, v>=0+w0∗v1+w1∗v2/2+…. Accordingly, <T∗w, v> does not equal <w, Tv>, and so T and T∗ are not even symmetric, which is a must in this case.#

In the previous example since the operator T is not self-adjoint, it automatically follows that the operator is not symmetric. The result does not hold for unbounded operators that in fact are the most important in quantum. For a not necessarily bounded operator on Hilbert space H, the domain of T, domT, is a subset of H. The adjoint T∗ has domain domT∗, which is also a subspace of H with vectors w such that there is a vector v in H such that <v, Tu>=<w, u>. By letting T∗w=v, define the adjoint operator T∗.

The graph of T is graph(T)={(v, Tv) such that v is in domT}. An operator S extends T means that graph(T) is a subset of graph(S). For a symmetric operator T, the graph(T) is a subset of the graph(T∗). The operator T is self-adjoint when graph(T)=graph(T∗). In this case, domT=domT∗ and T=T∗. A symmetric operator having domT=dom T∗ is self-adjoint.

A key theorem for quantum is the Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem stating that when T is defined on a Hilbert space for all v, w in H such that <Tv, w>=<v, T w>, then T must be bounded ([Teschl, 2009](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib17)). Since an everywhere-defined symmetric operator on H is also self-adjoint, then it follows that for a self-adjoint nonbounded operator T, its domain must be a proper subset of H. The operator T in this case must be a partially defined operator on H.

In several areas of quantum, operators are sometimes defined on a subset of a Hilbert, or a Banach space. This most often occurs for the adjoint operation, as well as for the closed operation. First, for the adjoint, T is defined on dom(T), which is a subset of Hilbert space *H*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si77.png), and T: *d**o**m*{*T*)→*H*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si78.png). *H*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si79.png) is another Hilbert space. In this case, T∗ is defined by T∗(u)=v, which means <v, w>=<u, T w>, for all w in the dom(T). In the above inner products, the first inner product is in *H*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si80.png) and the second is taken in *H*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si81.png). It is assumed that T∗ is a closed operator and that dom(T) is dense in *H*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si82.png). When this is true, <u, T v>=<T∗ u, v>, for v in dom(T) and u in dom(T∗). Similarly, assume that *B*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si83.png) and *B*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si84.png) are Banach spaces, and consider T in L (*B*[1],*B*[2])![Equation](Images/F000138si85.png). T is said to be a closed operator on dom(T), which is a subspace of B1 when given that vn converges to v in dom (T), and given that Tvn converges to w in *B*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si86.png), then w=Tv.

The operator T is said to be densely defined when dom(T) is dense in *B*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si87.png). T is fully defined when *d**o**m*(*T*) = *B*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si88.png). Closure of an operator T means that there exists a closed operator S, such that dom(T) is a subset of dom(S), and S=T on dom(T). Also, the graph norm on dom(T) is given for v in dom(T),‖v‖=‖v‖+‖T v‖; the first norm is taken in dom(T), the second in *B*[1]![Equation](Images/F000138si89.png), and the third in *B*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si90.png).

For a nonbounded operator T on a Hilbert space H, it is a closed operator when its graph is closed. The graph of T is a subset of the Cartesian product H x H. It is a vector space. The graph of T is Gr(T)={<v, T v>|v is in dom(T)}. The closed graph theorem says that an everywhere-defined linear map with a closed graph is continuous. See Appendix A.6. A partially defined linear map with a closed graph can be not continuous.

 

### Example 13.10

Consider the Hilbert space *H* = *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si91.png), that is, all complex-valued absolute sum squared sequences that converge. Let dom(T) be equal to all sequences such that the sum ∑|*n* *v**n*|²![Equation](Images/F000138si92.png) converges. Let T: dom (T)→H by Tv=T (v1, v2, v3, …)=(v1, 2v2, 3v3, …). The closure of dom(T)=H, so dom(T) is dense in H. This follows since dom(T) contains all sequences that have at most a finitely many nonzero terms. T is not one to one due to the finite number of nonzero terms. Two identical finite vector tuple strings in the range correspond to an infinite number of different terms in the domain whose image is the same finite tuple sequence. Additionally, T is unbounded, but it is self-adjoint, since <T∗w, v>=w1′∗v1+w2′∗v2+… and <w, Tv>=w1∗v1+w2∗2v2 +…. Here wk′∗ are tuples from T∗w. Then equating coefficients of vk gives wk′∗=wk/k. This means that T∗w=(w1, 2w2, 3w3, …). Moreover, the spectrum for T is the point spectrum: sppT={1, 2, 3, …} since Tvn=n vn.#

 

### Example 13.11

For the unbounded operator T, having an adjoint T∗ in the Hilbert space H with T: dom(T)→H. Let c∗ be in sppT∗. That is, c∗ is in the point spectrum of T∗. It will be seen that c will be in the union of sppT with sprT, specifically, that is, it will be in one of these. Since c∗ is an eigenvalue for T∗, there is an eigenvector v in dom(T∗) such that T∗v=c∗ v. For all w in dom(T), it follows that <v, Tw>=<T∗v, w>=<c∗v, w>=c <v, w>. So, <v, c w>−<v, Tw>=0, and because this holds for all w, this means that <v, (cI−T) w>=0 for all w in dom(T). Consequently, it follows that the ran(cI−T) is not dense, and so the spectrum cannot be continuous.#

 

### Example 13.12

Even though the position operation Q in *H* = *L*²(*R*)![Equation](Images/F000138si93.png) is unbounded, it is, however, self-adjoint. The inner product for f in H and the product x·g in H, where g is also in H, are given by the integral ∫[ − ∞]^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si94.png) f∗·(x·g) dx)=<f, x·g>. It follows that this quantity equals <x·f, g>. The latter inner product is the integral ∫[ − ∞]^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si95.png) (x·f∗)·g dx)=<x·f, g>. So Q(f)=x·f, and so the multiplication operator Q is self-adjoint.#

 

### Example 13.13

The momentum operator is also unbounded, but it too is self-adjoint in *H* = *L*²(*R*)![Equation](Images/F000138si96.png). The inner product in this case is <f, −id/dx g>; it is the integral ∫[ − ∞]^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si97.png) f∗·(−id/dx g) dx. Here it is assumed that the derivatives are integrable. Now integrating by parts gives (f∗·g) evaluated between minus infinity to plus infinity, along with the integral ∫[ − ∞]^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si98.png) (i d/dx f∗)·g dx. Assume that the product (f∗·g) goes to zero; then this result in terms of the inner product is <−id/dx f, g>, thus showing that this operator is also self-adjoint.#

 

## 13.4 Bounded operators and numerical range

As mentioned in [Section 7.1](#Ch007_131-144_B9780443136979000205.xhtml#s0010), the numerical range is very useful in characterizing the types of spectra associated with bounded operators on Hilbert space. To see this, consider the operator T in the Banach space or actually the C∗ algebra, B(H). The numerical range for an operator T is sup[*∥**v**∥* = 1]![Equation](Images/F000138si99.png) <v, T v>. Assume that cI−T is not invertible, and it is not even one to one. Then, there exists v nonzero in H with (T−I c) v=0. Use this identity, Tv=c v, and form the inner product with v, <v, Tv>=c <v, v>, where‖v‖=1. This shows that the eigenvalue c is in the numerical range. As a consequence, the point spectrum sppT is a subset of the numerical range.

Now assume that the range of (c−T) is not dense in H; this means that the closure clos(c−T) is a proper subset A of H. Then there exists a unit vector w in *A*^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si100.png), such that the inner product <w, (T−c) w>=0, that is, <w, T w>=c. So again c is in the numerical range. Thus, the residual spectrum sprT is part of the numerical range of T.

Lastly, assume that the range of (T−c) is dense in H, but not equal to H. In this situation, there exists a sequence of normalized vectors, *w*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si101.png) in H such that (T−c) *w*[*n*]→0![Equation](Images/F000138si102.png). A sequence going to zero has to exist. Otherwise, (T−c) would be bounded from below, and as seen in [Section 7.6](#Ch007_131-144_B9780443136979000205.xhtml#s0035) and earlier in this chapter, dense and bounded from below implies (T−c) is invertible. Using the inner product with the sequence *w*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si103.png) gives <*w*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si104.png), (T−c) *w*[*n*] >  =  < *w*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si105.png), T *w*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si106.png)  >  − *c* < *w*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si107.png), *w*[*n*]\>→0![Equation](Images/F000138si108.png). As a consequence, this time c is in the closure of the numerical range. In this case, the continuous spectrum spcT is a subset of the closure of the numerical range.

A list of properties for the numerical range W(T) for n by n complex -valued matrix are provided as follows ([Gustafson and Rao, 1997](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib5)):

1.  1) W (T) is a compact subset of C.
2.  2) W (T) is a convex set in C, by the Hausdorff-Toeplitz theorem.
3.  3) W (T) contains the spectrum of T.
4.  4) If T=T∗, then W (T) is the closed interval on the real line. Moreover, it consists of end points that are two eigenvalues of T.

The next example illustrates the use of eigenvalues for finding the numerical range. It also illustrates Property 4). This same example was solved by numerical simulation in Example 7.3 where a most general qubit in *C*²![Equation](Images/F000138si109.png) was inserted into the numerical range formula.

 

### Example 13.14

The eigenvalues for the self-adjoint matrix T=

$\\begin{matrix} {|2} & {i|} \\\\ {|{- i}} & {1|} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000138si110.png)

are found from the solution of the characteristic equation: *t*² − 3*t* + 1 = 0![Equation](Images/F000138si111.png). The eigenvalues are (3+−5^(1/2))/2. = .382, 2.618![Equation](Images/F000138si112.png). The numerical range is W (T)=\[.382, 2.618\].#

More generally, for an operator T on Hilbert space H, several other properties hold for the numerical range ([Shapiro, 2004](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib15)).

1.  1) W (T) is invariant under unitary similarity.
2.  2) W (T) lies in the closed disk of radius ‖T‖ centered at the origin.
3.  3) W (T∗)={c∗ for all c in W (T)}.
4.  4) W (I)={1}.
5.  5) For a, b in C, and T in B(H), W (a T+b I)=a W (T)+b.
6.  6) If T is nilpotent, that is, *T*^(*n* + 1) = 0![Equation](Images/F000138si113.png), then the spectrum of T is zero in clos W (T).

 

### Example 13.15

Use as the carrier set the algebra of 2 by 2 complex-valued matrices T. If T is the matrix with all zeros except for the first row second column entry, here, let entry *T*[1, 2]![Equation](Images/F000138si114.png) be equal to one, T=

$\\begin{matrix} {|0} & {1|} \\\\ {|0} & {0|} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000138si115.png)

Then sp(T)=0 and ‖T‖=1. Additionally, T is nilpotent order two since T²\=0.#

For unbounded operators, relations between the spectrum and the numerical range are the following: ([StackExchange, 2015](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib16)).

1.  1) If T is normal, then the whole spectrum of T lies in the clos W (T∗).
2.  2) If T is symmetric, contained in closT contained in T∗, then the spectrum need not be real, but closW (T) is a subset of R.
3.  3) If T is not a closed operator, and T is a subset of closT=T∗∗, then the spectrum is complex and it contains the closW (T).

For a self-adjoint bounded operator T on H, there is a relationship between the numerical range W(T) and an eigenvalue of T. When a=inf<v, Tv> for all ‖v‖=1, then a is in spT ([Gustafson and Rao, 1997](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib5)).

As mentioned earlier, the real part of the dissipative operator T in a Hilbert space H is one such that for all v in H, the real part of the numerical range is nonpositive. That is, Re <v, Tv> is nonpositive, with ‖v‖=1. The next few examples will illustrate this concept.

 

### Example 13.16

Let the carrier set for the Hilbert space be *H* = *R*^(*n*)![Equation](Images/F000138si116.png), with the usual inner product if T=−I, that is the negative of the diagonal identity matrix; then for all v in *H*,  < *v*, *T* *v* >  =  − ∥*v*∥²![Equation](Images/F000138si117.png), as such T is dissipative.#

 

### Example 13.17

Another instance of a dissipating operator T this time in *L*²(*R*)![Equation](Images/F000138si118.png) intersects *C**o*¹(*R*)![Equation](Images/F000138si119.png). This is the space consisting of continuously differentiable functions of compact support, which are absolutely square integrable. Let T be a momentum type operator, T=d/dt.

Then <T f, f>=integral, ∫[*t* =  − ∞]^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si120.png) f′∗ f dt, where the prime stands for derivative. Now integrating by parts gives <T f, f>=∫[*t* =  − ∞]^∞![Equation](Images/F000138si121.png)−f∗ f′dt=− <f, T f>=− <Tf, f> ∗. So the real part of <T f, f>=0, because when z=− z∗, z is pure imaginary. Accordingly, T is dissipative.#

In a Banach space A, the definition of an operator T being dissipative is extended because there need not be an inner product. In this case, if for all c> 0 and all v in dom(T),‖(c−T) v‖is greater than or equal to c‖v‖; then T is dissipative. A quite complete compilation of dissipative operators in a Banach space is in [Lumer and Philips (1961)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib9) and [Engel and Nangel (2000)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib4). These properties are needed in proving the Lumer-Phillips theorem previously mentioned relating the spectrum of an operator with the spectrum of its dual operator.

Whenever Re <v, Tv> is nonnegative, with‖v‖=1, T is called an accretive operator. Applications to these, as well as dissipative operators, are in creating one-parameter semigroups, much like in Stone’s theorem. In the present case, the semigroup consists of operators in a Banach space of the form, *e*^(*t**T*)![Equation](Images/F000138si122.png), when a dissipative operator is utilized. The corresponding operators in a Banach space are of the form *e*^( − *t**T*)![Equation](Images/F000138si123.png) whenever the generator is an accretive operator T. However, many of these operators are partially defined ([Delaubenfels, 1988](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib3)).

 

## 13.5 Self-adjoint operators

As previously mentioned, this and the next section provide a review as well as an extension of concepts related to self-adjoint operators. Of most importance, in quantum disciplines, observables are operators in a C∗ algebra, A. They are self-adjoint operators T, such that T=T∗. Moreover, these operators are measurable and defined via RRT, similar to the procedure of finding the dual space. The method is very similar to the creation of the adjoint T∗, for the case where T: H→H was considered previously.

Suppose that T: H1→H2, where H1 and H2 are Hilbert spaces. Additionaly assume for now that T is bounded, that is, T is in B (H1, H2). As in the dual space development, a functional f will be defined. It is such that for fixed w in H2, f: H1→C, where for any v in H1 it follows that f (v)=<w, T v>. The functional is linear and bounded since T is bounded and also|f (v)|is less than or equal to‖w‖‖T v‖. This inequality is a direct result of the CBS inequality. Additionally, the last expression is less than or equal to‖w‖‖T‖‖v‖since T is bounded. Moreover f is in the dual space of H1.

Using RRT, for every w in H2, there is a unique u in H1 such that f (v)=<u, v>, holding for all v in H1. This defines a mapping: T∗: H2→H1, which is called the adjoint of T, mentioned previously in the last section. The mapping T∗ is given by T∗ (w)=u. In short, the defining property of T∗ is <w, T v>=<T∗ w, v>, for all v in H1 and w in H2. The first inner product mentioned earlier is in H2, and the second is in H1. Since T is assumed to be bounded, it follows that T∗ is also linear and bounded, that is, T∗ is in B (H2, H1). In addition, the following holds for T and T∗.

1.  1) Norm equality: ‖T∗‖=‖T‖.
2.  2) Involution: (T∗)∗=T.
3.  3) Commuting norm: ∥*T* *T*\*∥=∥*T*\**T*∥=∥*T*∥²![Equation](Images/F000138si124.png).
4.  4) Inverse: If T is invertible, then so is T∗ and (T^(−1))∗=(T∗)^(−1).
5.  5) Additive: (S+T)∗=S∗+T∗, where S is also in B (H1, H2).
6.  6) Anticommutative: S∗ T∗=(T S)∗.

A unique representation involving self-adjoint operators can be made for a bounded operator T. Let Q and S be self-adjoint operators in the C∗ algebra A; then T can be represented as T=Q+iS. Therefore T∗=Q−iS. Adding T plus T∗ and then subtracting T∗ from T gives Q=(T+T∗)/2 and S=(T−T∗)/ (2i), respectively. The operators Q and S can be thought to be the real and imaginary parts of T, in that order.

If K is a closed subspace of H, then K is itself a Hilbert space. In this case, any vector v in H can be written as u+w, where <u, w>=0 and u is in K. The space of all those vectors orthogonal to vectors in K is called K perp, that is, write it as perp(K) or *K*^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si125.png). A projection operator P can be associated with this procedure. Indeed, let P: H→K, where P (v)=u. Such an operation is both idempotent and self-adjoint. Note that (I−P) (v)=w. If also v′=u′+w′ with u′ in K and w′ in perp(K), then <P(v), v′>=<u, u′>=<v, u′>=<v, P(v′)>. Furthermore, <u, w>=<P(v), (I−P)(v)>=<v, P (I−P) (v)>=0. When K is a closed subspace of H, then perp(K) is also closed. An important property of a vector subspace K of a Hilbert space H is that the closure of K equals perp(perp(K)). If K is a closed subspace of H, then again K=perp(perp(K)). Moreover, K is closed iff *K* = (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si126.png). To see this, first assume that *K* = (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si127.png). Then choose a sequence *v*[*n*]→*v*![Equation](Images/F000138si128.png), where *v*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si129.png) is in K and v is in H. It will be shown that v is in K. Take w in *K*^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si130.png), then <w, *v*[*n*] >  = 0![Equation](Images/F000138si131.png) for all n, and then using the continuity of an inner product: lim[*n* → ∞] < *w*![Equation](Images/F000138si132.png), *v*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si133.png)\>=<w, lim[*n* → ∞]*v*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000138si134.png)\>=<w, v>=0. This shows that v is in *K* = (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si135.png), and so K is closed.

Going the other way, if K is a closed subspace of H, then *K* = (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si136.png) will be shown. Taking the inner product of v in K and any w in *K*^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si137.png) gives <v, w>=<w, v>∗=0, thus showing v is also in (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si138.png). So K is a subset of (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si139.png). To see the opposite set inclusion, let v be in (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si140.png). Then represent v=w+z, where w is in K and z is in *K*^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si141.png). Using linearity, 0=<v, z>=<w, z>+<z, z>=0+<z, z>=‖z‖², which implies that z=0. Accordingly, v=w and so (*K*^⊥)^⊥![Equation](Images/F000138si142.png) is a subset of K, and therefore they are equal.

When T is bounded, there is a relation between the kernel and the image of the adjoint operation, namely Ker(T)=perp(Im(T∗)) and also that the closure of Im(T∗)=perp(ker(T)). Additionally, if K is closed, then perp(K)=perp(closure(K))=closure(perp(K)). Also, perp(perp(K))=closure(K). For a closed subspace K, it follows that perp(perp(K))=K. Moreover, using w=u+v, then for P in B(H) and P(w)=u, ∥*P*(*w*)∥² = ∥*w*∥² − ∥*w* − *u*∥²![Equation](Images/F000138si143.png); this follows, because w−u=v and <u, v>=0. So, ∥*u*∥² = ∥*w* − *v*∥² = ∥*w*∥² − ∥*v*∥²![Equation](Images/F000138si144.png).

Relations between the adjoint and the kernel are as follows:

1.  1) Ker(T∗)=perp(ran(T)).
2.  2) Perp(ker(T∗))=clos(ran(T)).

An example will be given using the basis for a momentum operator, the derivative operation. It will illustrate a closed operator on a subspace of a Hilbert space, where this operator is not bounded.

 

### Example 13.18

Consider the Lebesgue space of square absolute value integrable complex-valued functions on \[0, 1\]. It is denoted by *L*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si145.png) \[0, 1\]. Again, let the unbounded momentum type operator T be employed where T=d /dx. Then, the domain of T is D(T) where *D*(*T*) = {*f* *i**n* *L*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si146.png) \[0, 1\], such that f is absolutely continuous, where d f /dx is in *L*[2]![Equation](Images/F000138si147.png) \[0, 1\] with f(0)=0}. Then T is closed in D(T) ([Park, 2013](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib11)). It is not closed in the Banach space C\[0, 1\]. That is, it is not closed in the domain {f in C\[0, 1\], such that d f /dx is in C \[0, 1\] with f(0)=0}. See Example 8.1 for details.#

In a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, the adjoint operator is guaranteed to exist by RRT; however, in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space H, the adjoint may not exist at all. Sometimes it will exist and be of little use. First of all, the adjoint will exist when and only when T is densely defined. In this way, RRT can be used on the inner product showing existence and uniqueness of the adjoint operation. The adjoint is of great use whenever the adjoint itself, T∗, is densely defined, and this is when T is closable. The definition of the adjoint is given as follows: For all v in dom(T) and for all u in dom(T∗), then the inner products are equal, <u, Tv>=<T∗u, v>. Because, the closure of the domain of T=clos(dom(T))=H, therefore T∗ will uniquely be found for u in dom(T∗).

Consider a vector u in H; if there is a w in H such that <u, Tv>=<w, v> for all v in dom(T), then <u, Tv> is a continuous linear form on dom(T). When <u, Tv> is continuous on dom(T), it can be extended by continuity on all of H. Next, RRT can be applied showing there is a unique w in H such that <u, Tv>=<w, v>. The result follows when and only when dom(T) is dense in H. This shows the adjoint exists and is unique when T is bounded.

 

## 13.6 Normal operators and nonbounded operators

The spectrum of a bounded operator is compact and nonempty; therefore, it is closed and bounded in the complex plane. Because of these properties, the spectral radius r (T) can be defined for T in A. It is r (T)=sup {|c|, such thatc is in the spectrum of T}. Additionally, the supremal radius is achieved for some c in sp(T), and also r (T) is less than or equal to‖T‖. Moreover, the spectrum can be found using the Gelfand formula: r (T)=limit as n goes to infinity for ∥*T*^(*n*)∥^(1/*n*)![Equation](Images/F000138si148.png). When the operator T is normal, it follows that the spectral radius is the norm, that is, r (T)=‖T‖. As a consequence, if T is in a C∗ algebra, then‖T‖²\=r (T∗ T).

 

### Example 13.19

Because a self-adjoint operator T, H:→H is normal, the spectral radius of T equals its norm that is r (T)=‖T‖. So, for instance, if spT=0, this implies that T=0. Note that the operator T=

$\\begin{matrix} {|0} & {1|} \\\\ {|0} & {0|} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000138si149.png)

The spectrum spT=0, but T is not zero, nor is it a normal operator.#

In general, however, the spectral radius can be smaller than the norm, as seen, for instance, using nilpotent operators.

Previously for a bounded operator T in the C∗ algebra A, it was seen that T can be represented using two self-adjoint operators Q and S, as T=Q+iS. Therefore, T∗=Q−iS. Multiplying T by its adjoint T∗ gives T T∗=Q²+i(S Q−Q S)+S². Next multiplying T∗ T=Q²+i(−S Q+Q S)+S². So whenever S Q−Q S=−S Q+Q S, that is, when S Q=Q S, it follows that T is a normal operator. Another interesting property of a normal operator is given in the following example.

 

### Example 13.20

If T is a normal operator in a C∗ algebra, then ‖T²‖=‖T‖². To see this, use the C∗ identity ‖T∗ T‖=‖T‖² from [Section 3.8](#Ch003_41-55_B9780443136979000175.xhtml#s0045); then it follows that ‖(T∗ T)²‖=‖T‖⁴. On the other hand, squaring ‖T²‖ gives ‖T²‖², and applying the C∗ identity to this quantity leads to the equation ‖T²‖²\=‖(T∗)² T²‖. Employing the normality condition winds up with ‖T²‖²\=‖(T∗ T)²‖. So‖T‖⁴\=‖T²‖², and taking square roots completes the proof.

A distinct proof uses the spectral radius. As mentioned earlier, let *r* = *l**i**m**i**t*[*n* → ∞]![Equation](Images/F000138si150.png) ∥*T*^(*n*)![Equation](Images/F000138si151.png) ∥^(1/*n*)![Equation](Images/F000138si152.png). For integer n larger than zero, ∥*T*^(2^(*n*))![Equation](Images/F000138si153.png) ∥² = ∥(*T*^(2^(*n*))) \* *T*^(2^(*n*))∥ = ∥(*T*\**T*)^(2^(*n*))∥ = ∥*T*∥^(2^(*n* + 1))![Equation](Images/F000138si154.png). So, by mathematical induction ∥*T*^(2^(*n*))∥ = ∥*T*∥^(2^(*n*))![Equation](Images/F000138si155.png), for all n larger than zero. By Gelfands formula, *r* = *l**i**m**i**t*[*n* → ∞]∥*T*^(2^(*n*))∥^(2^( − *n*)) = ∥*T*∥![Equation](Images/F000138si156.png).#

For normal operators T, the residual spectrum, that is sprT is nonexistent ([Conway, 1990](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib2)). So the spectrum is comprised of the point and continuous spectrums only. This will be seen again in a later section. Moreover, normal operators have numerical radius the same as spectral radius. There is a close relation between a nonzero normal operator T in a C∗ algebra and the states within a C∗ algebra. For every such operator T, there exists a state g where *g*(*T*\**T*) = ∥*T*∥²![Equation](Images/F000138si157.png) and |g (T)|=‖T‖. For every such nonzero normal operator T in A, there exists a pure state g where |g (T)|=‖T‖.

The set of all compact operators on H forms a C∗ algebra. It is nonunital in the infinite-dimensional case. However, an approximate identity can be developed, since this structure is isomorphic to the space of square summable sequences, *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si158.png) ([Murphy, 2014](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib10)).

For two nonbounded operators S and T on H, T is an extension of S whenever dom(S) is a subset of dom(T) and S (v)=T (v) for all v in dom(S). Here, S is said to be a restriction of T. So, S is said to be closable if it has a closed extension T. A core of a closed operator T is a subspace X contained in the dom(T) when T is the closure extending dom(T) intersecting X. The core is also called the essential domain; it is such that for v in dom(T) there exists a sequence vn in X such that‖v−vn‖+‖Tv−Tvn‖→0 as n→∞![Equation](Images/F000138si159.png) ([Reed and Simon, 1980](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib12)).

For any nonbounded operator T on H that is also closable, the closure of T denoted by closT is defined to be the smallest closed extension. It is given by the intersection of all closed sets containing T, and additionally, closT is unique. For T densely defined on dom(T) in H, T is called symmetric, which means that <u, Tv>=<Tu, v> for all u and v in dom(T). A symmetric densely defined unbounded operator T has closure: closT=T∗∗. Nonsymmetric operators need not be closable. It is easy to use a test for the self-adjoint criteria of a closed symmetric operator T. It is that the intersection of the resolvent set of T and R is nonempty ([Woozy, 2017](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib19)).

An operator T on H is symmetric, which means that <T x, y>=<x, T y> for all x and y in the dom(T). This means that dom(T) is contained in the dom(T∗). A symmetric operator is such that T is a subset of T∗∗, which itself is a subset of T∗. The operator T is symmetric also iff the numerical range of T is real, that is, W (T) is a subset of R. When T is bounded and if for all v, w in H <v, T w> is real, then T is symmetric. For closed symmetric operators, the following holds: T=T∗∗ is a subset of T∗. A rigorous treatment involving all important domain issues can be found in [Hall (2013)](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib8).

A closable operator T is said to be essentially self-adjoint whenever it has self-adjoint closure. It is essentially self-adjoint iff it is symmetric, densely defined and there exists a nonreal complex number c, such that c−T and c∗−T have dense range. For a bounded self-adjoint operator T, with smallest spectral value a and largest spectral value b, it follows that a=−‖T‖, or b=‖T‖. Moreover, the closure of the numerical range=\[a, b\]. Additionally, the self-adjoint operator T is positive when W (T) or spT lies in the nonnegative real line. The set of all positive operators in a C∗ algebra A is a convex cone in a real vector space V={T in A, such that T=T∗|.

For a self-adjoint operator T, on Hilbert space H, it follows that ker(T+−i)={0}. In order to see this, first assume that Tv=iv. Then <v, Tv>=<v, iv>=i <v, v>, and also <Tv, v>=<iv, v>=−i <v, v>, but since T is self-adjoint, it follows that ker(T+−i)={0}. The same is true for T∗, that is, ker(T∗+−i)={0}. When T is symmetric and closed with ker(T+−i)={0}, then ran(T+−i)=H. It will be shown that ran(T+−i) is dense in H. For v in perp(ran(T+i)) and for all w in dom(T). it follows that <v, (T+i)w>=0. So, in this case, <v, Tw>=<−iv, w>. For v in the dom(T∗) and (T∗+i)v=0, therefore v is in ker(T∗+i). Also notice that ∥(*T*+*i*)*v*∥² =  < (*T*+*i*)*v*, (*T*+*i*)*v* >  = ∥*T**v*∥² + ∥*v*∥²![Equation](Images/F000138si160.png). Consequently, if (T+i)vn is a CS, then it follows that Tvn is a CS and also vn is a CS. When vn converges to v since T is closed, v is in dom(T) and Tvn→Tv.

Unbounded operators should be closed and densely defined. As mentioned previously, the closed graph theorem and the concepts associated with this construct play an important role in determining closure of operators. As an instance of the closed graph theorem determining closure, consider the example.

 

### Example 13.21

For the densely defined self-adjoint operator T=T∗, it follows that T is closed. Begin with the identity <T∗ u, v>=<u, T v>. In terms of the relation, (u, w) is in the graph of T∗, which means that <w, v>=<u, Tv> for all v in dom(T). By using continuity w→<w, v> and u→<u, Tv> shows that the set of all (u, w) in T∗ is closed. Therefore, T∗ is closed, but T=T∗ and so T is also closed.#

A densely defined symmetric operator T with dom(T) a subset of H→H is self-adjoint iff the ran(T+iI)=ran(T−iI)=H. First notice that to be symmetric means that dom(T) is contained in dom(T∗). Assume that the identities involving the range equaling H hold. Next, it is shown that dom(T∗) is contained in dom(T). So let w be in dom(T∗). We must show that w is also in dom(T). Then there exists an element v in H such that for any u in dom(T), <w, (T+i)u>=<v, u>. Now because ran(T−i)=H it follows that v=(T−i)z for some z in dom(T). Because T is symmetric and u is also in dom(T), it follows that <w, (T+i)u>=<v, u>=<(T−i)z, u>=<Tz, u>+i<z, u>=<z, Tu>+<z, iu>=<z, (T+i)u>, but ran(T+i)=H; this implies that w=z since z is in dom(T); then w is in dom(T). So dom(T)=dom(T∗).#

Symmetric densely defined operator T, on Hilbert space H, can be self-adjoint whenever T+−i is injective; then T∗+−iI becomes an extension, i.e., a bijection from dom(T) onto H. Here T=T∗. The problem for T being only symmetric and not self-adjoint is that T+−iI is not necessarily surjective. There exist self-adjoint extensions for T whenever the deficiency indices of T are equal, and only then. These indices are given by dim(ran(perp(T+iI))) and dim(ran(perp(T−iI))) and are mentioned again in the context of partial isometrics. Partial isometries are linear maps between Hilbert spaces. It is an isometry on the orthogonal complement of its kernel. Whenever the indices are the same, these extensions can be parametrized by using linear isometrics or by the use of the Cayley transformation mentioned earlier ([Hall, 2013](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib8)).

For a symmetric operator T, there are relationships between X=dim(perp(T+i)) and Y=dim(perp(T−i)) and unique self-adjoint or essentially self-adjoint extensions of T. When X=Y=0, these extensions exist. When X=Y is greater than or equal to one, then T has infinitely many self-adjoint extensions. When X differs from Y, then T has no self-adjoint extensions. In any case, whenever T is essentially self-adjoint, then the closure of T, clos(T), is the unique self-adjoint extension of T. This can be seen because if S=S∗ then since a self-adjoint operator is always closed, it follows that dom(S∗) is a subset of dom(clos(T)), which is a subset of dom(S). Since S is self-adjoint, all three domains are equal and so S=clos(T).

The square root of a positive operator P is a self-adjoint operator T, such that *P* = *T*²![Equation](Images/F000138si161.png). For any bounded operator P, there is a unique positive square root, it is denoted|T|, and it is the positive square root of T∗T. Also the polar decomposition can be performed involving a unique partial isometry U and |T|. Here, T=U|T|, and ker(T∗) is a subset of Ker(U). The same results hold for unbounded operators provided that they are closed and densely defined. In this case, |T| could be unbounded. It is a nonnegative self-adjoint operator with the same domain as T. Also U is a partial isometry such that U=0 on perp(Im(T)). In finite dimensions, however, U can be extended to a unitary operator ([Wells and Williams, 2012](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib18)). In infinite dimensions, it is not true that a partial isometry can be extended to a unitary operation. For instance, the left-shift operator L: *l*² → {(*x*[2], *x*[3],…)![Equation](Images/F000138si162.png) in *l*²}![Equation](Images/F000138si163.png) is an isometry on the subspace S={x in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si164.png), where *x*[1]\=0}![Equation](Images/F000138si165.png). So *L*:*S*→*l*²![Equation](Images/F000138si166.png) and is onto.

A simple result for bounded, self-adjoint operators T extends eigenvalue and eigenvector consequences of self-adjoint or Hermitian matrices. Indeed, let a and b be in the point spectrum of T, sppT. The associated eigenvectors v and w are nonzero and such that Tv=av and Tw=bw. When a is different from b; then v is orthogonal to w, since <T v, w>=a <v, w>=<v, T w>=b <v, w>, and (a−b) <v, w>=0, but a−b is not zero. Thus, <v, w>=0. For any self-adjoint operator, it follows that T=T∗=T∗∗. Additionally, a closed symmetric operator is self-adjoint iff T∗ is symmetric.

 

## 13.7 Spectral decomposition

The spectral decomposition for bounded self-adjoint operators T on the complex Hilbert space H will be described next. These operators are fundamental in quantum since all observables are of this form. For continuous functions f and g, defined on the spectrum of T, and a and b real scalars, the following identities involving T must uphold:

1.  1) Linear: (a f+b g) (T)=a f (T)+b g (T).
2.  2) Product: (f g) (T)=f (T) g (T).
3.  3) Identity: I (T)=I.
4.  4) Adjoint: f∗ (T)=f (T).
5.  5) Spectral Invariance: For eigenvalue c of T and v in H, if T v=c v, then this implies that f (T) v=f (c) v.
6.  6) Spectrum: The spectrum of f (T)={f (c) is such that c is in the spectrum of T}.
7.  7) Positive: f greater or equal to zero implies f (T) is greater or equal to zero.

 

### Example 13.22

This is another example involving the residual spectrum for a bounded operator T, in Hilbert space H. It makes for an interesting example of an eigenvector. In this case, if c is in sprT, then the conjugate value c∗ is in sppT∗. First, since c is in the residual spectrum of T, then ran(cI−T) is not dense in nor equal to H; it is a subspace. Then, there has to exist a nonzero vector v in H, which is not in clos(cI−T). This element is in the null space of (c∗I−T∗) and is such that for arbitrary w in H, <v, (cI−T) w>=<(c∗I−T∗) v, w>=0. Since w is arbitrary, (c∗I−T∗) v=0, implying that c∗ is an eigenvalue for T∗ and so c∗ is in sppT∗.#

## 13.8 Spectra for self-adjoint, normal, and compact operators

It was seen that for a self-adjoint operator in B(H), there is no residual spectrum, and moreover, the spectrum is always real. Approximate eigenvalues of an operator in B(H) are such that for any *ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000138si173.png)\> 0, there exists a unit vector v in H, such that ‖Tv−*λ*v‖<*ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000138si174.png). Replacing v by w /‖w‖for w not zero, the equivalent condition is as follows: For any *ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000138si175.png)\> 0, there exists a nonzero vector w in H, such that ‖Tw−*λ*w‖<![ent](Images/epsi_1013.png)‖w‖; then *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si176.png) is an approximate eigenvalue for T. The set of all such *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si177.png) for T is called the approximate spectrum of T. It will be denoted by A(T). If T has an eigenvalue, then it is in A(T) since Tv−*λ*v is identically zero. Additionally, A(T) is a true spectrum since A(T) is a subset of spT. The result follows by contradiction. If *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si178.png) is not in spT, then T−*λ*I is invertible. This implies that ∥*v*∥ = ∥(*T*−*λ**I*)^( − 1)![Equation](Images/F000138si179.png) (T−*λ*I) v‖is less than or equal to ∥(*T*−*λ**I*)^( − 1)∥∥*T**v* − *λ**v*∥![Equation](Images/F000138si180.png) for every vector v, that is, ∥*T**v* − *λ**v*∥![Equation](Images/F000138si181.png) is greater than or equal to 1/∥(*T*−*λ**I*)^( − 1)∥∥*v*∥![Equation](Images/F000138si182.png). Letting *ϵ* = 1/∥(*T*−*λ**I*)^( − 1)![Equation](Images/F000138si183.png)‖ shows that ‖Tv−*λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si184.png) v‖is bounded below, and therefore *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si185.png) is not in A(T), which is a contradiction. So the conclusion is that A(T) is always a subset of spT.

For bounded normal operators, even more is true besides the result mentioned earlier; here, spT=A(T), this was mentioned previously. That is, for a normal operator T, all eigenvalues are approximate. What must be shown is that spT is a subset of A(T). Again contradiction will be employed. First say that there is an eigenvalue *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si186.png) in spT, which is not in A(T). Then for some *ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000138si187.png)\> 0, this eigenvalue is such that ‖Tw−*λ*w‖ is greater or equal to ![ent](Images/epsi_1013.png)‖w‖ for all v nonzero. Since T is normal, it follows that ‖T∗w−*λ*∗w‖ is greater or equal to ![ent](Images/epsi_1013.png)‖w‖ for all v nonzero. So both ‖Tw−*λ*w‖ and ‖T∗w−*λ*∗w‖ are bounded below, see [Section 13.1](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#s0010). If it can be shown that their ranges are dense, then a contradiction occurs, because then, in particular, Tw−*λ*w would be invertible. Instead of showing the range to be dense, it is equivalent, showing that the orthogonal complement of the range is {0}. This follows since *r**a**n*(*u*)^⊥ = ker (*u*\*)![Equation](Images/F000138si188.png), or ker (*u*\*)^⊥ = *c**l**o**s*(*r**a**n*(*u*)![Equation](Images/F000138si189.png). So if v isorthogonal to Tw−*λ*w, that is, <v, Tw−*λ*w>=0 for all w, using the adjoint, this is the same as <T∗v- *λ*∗v, w>=0 for all w. The latter equation implies that T∗w−*λ*∗w=0. However, using the previous bounded below property ∥*T* \* *w* − *λ* \* *w*∥![Equation](Images/F000138si190.png) is greater than or equal to *ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000138si191.png)‖w‖shows that w=0.#

For normal operators, it is easy to show the relationship between eigenvalues of T and of T∗. The example below illustrates this fact

 

### Example 13.24

For T, a normal operator in B(H), if *T**v* = *λ**v*![Equation](Images/F000138si192.png) for nonzero v in H, then *T* \* *v* = *λ*^(\*)*v*![Equation](Images/F000138si193.png). This follows by letting A consist of all eigenvectors of T for which *λ*![Equation](Images/F000138si194.png) is an eigenvalue. Then since T(T∗v)=T∗(Tv)=T∗(*λ*v)=*λ*(T∗v), it follows that T∗v is in A. For compact self-adjoint operators T, on a Hilbert space H, the spectrum is a real-valued point spectrum with the possible exception of zero. The point zero might be an accumulation point, and therefore it might not be in the point spectrum. In this case, it is in the continuous spectrum. Again, the operator T can be represented as a converging sum of projections onto the eigenspace {an, such that Tv=an, for v nonzero in H}. That is, Pn is the projection onto this eigenspace and an, and T is the sum, ∑![Equation](Images/F000138si195.png) (an Pn). Also, for any w in H, it follows that Tw is equal to the sum, ∑![Equation](Images/F000138si196.png) (an Pn(w)).

 

### Example 13.25

Consider a compact self-adjoint operator T on a Hilbert space H. It is possible that such an operator only has a point spectrum with eigenvalue 0. Accordingly, in this situation, 0 is not a point of accumulation; it is an isolated point. By the projection theorem for normal compact operators, perp(ker(T)) cannot be infinite. For if it had an infinite ON basis {ek} with Tek=ck ek, and ck→0, then 0 is not isolated ([Conway, 1990](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib2)). Therefore, perp(ker(T)) is finite and so Ker(T)=0 has infinite dimension. It also follows that there exist countable infinite vectors, all with 0 as their eigenvalue.#

If T and S are compact operators on H, the product TS and ST are compact, as well as the adjoint S∗ and T∗. Moreover, T∗T is self-adjoint and positive; as such, it has nonnegative eigenvalues an. A compact operator T is said to be of trace class whenever the one norm of T is finite. The one norm is ‖T‖ and is such that the summation of the square root of each an, the eigenvalues of T∗T, is finite.

For a trace class operator T, the trace is defined as before: Tr (T) is the sum of the inner products: <en, T en>, where en is an ON basis on H. Additionally, the series must converge absolutely and independently of the ON basis employed. When T is also self-adjoint, then Tr (T)=sum of the real eigenvalues of T. Also, for a unitary operator U on H, it follows that the trace: *T**r*(*T*) = *T**r*(*U*^( − 1)*T* *U*)![Equation](Images/F000138si197.png). See [Section 7.5](#Ch007_131-144_B9780443136979000205.xhtml#s0030).

 

## 13.9 Pure states and density functions

The most important trace class operator previously given is the pure state Rz. It is also called a density operator, because it acts like a probability density function when forming expected values. As such, it is nonnegative and Tr (Rz)=1. The eigenvalues an of Rz are in (0, 1\]. The projection Pn onto the eigenspace is Rz, and it equals the sum ∑![Equation](Images/F000138si198.png) (an Pn) where the sum of all the an equals one.

A state is defined to be a linear functional g on a C∗ algebra A. That is, g: A→C. It must also satisfy:

1.  1) Nonnegative: g (T∗ T) is greater or equal to zero for all T in A.
2.  2) Identity: g (I)=1.

It can be shown that if g is linear functional on A, where g (I)=‖g‖=1, then g is a state. That is, the nonnegativity can be obtained from the norm of g equaling one ([Murphy, 2014](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib10)).

Some useful facts concerning any nonnegative linear functional g, on a C∗ algebra A will be listed. Here, T and S are operators in A, often called observables, and I is the identity operator in A:

1.  1) CBS Type Inequality: |*g*(*T*\**S*)|²![Equation](Images/F000138si199.png) is less than or equal to g (T∗ T) g (S∗ S).
2.  2) Conjugate: g (S∗)=g (S)∗.
3.  3) One Law: g (I)=‖g‖.
4.  4) Norm Bound: g (T∗ S∗ S T) is less than or equal to ∥*S*∥²*g*(*T*\**T*)![Equation](Images/F000138si200.png) ([Murphy, 2014](#Ch013_231-253_B9780443136979000138.xhtml#bib10)).

The norm bound is a type of CBS inequality. Pure states were described previously in several different ways. One of them bears a ray involving a convex set within a vector space. Recall that a convex set S is such that for any two vectors u and v in S the line segment joining these two vectors lies wholly in S also. That is, a v+(1−a) u is in S for all a in \[0, 1\]. An extreme point occurs when a v+(1−a)u=w and u=v=w for all a in (0, 1). So an extreme point on a convex line segment is an end point of that segment. In a C∗ algebra, the set of extreme points are called pure states and belong to a space of bounded operators over a Hilbert space. An example will be given.

 

### Example 13.26

The trace on a C∗ algebra A is a positive linear functional f: A→C such that for all T and S in A:

1.  1) The trace property holds f (TS)=f (ST).
2.  2) Positive means f (T∗ T) is greater than or equal to zero for T in A. Moreover, whenever f (T∗ T)=0 only when T=0, the trace is said to be faithful. Faithful means for a positive map g, if S is greater or equal to zero and g (S)=0, then it must be that S=0.

The unital associative algebra of all n by n complex-valued matrices is a C∗ algebra, and the trace is the sum of the diagonal elements, Tr(|a><b|)=<b, a>. So, for instance, in *C*²![Equation](Images/F000138si201.png), if a=(2 i)′ and b=(3 4i)′, then <b, a>=10. The outer product, T=a><b, is given below with T∗T the conjugate symmetric matrix with positive trace:

$\\begin{matrix} \\left| 100 \\right. & \\left. - 80i \\right| & \\left| 45 \\right. & \\left. - 60i \\right| \\\\ \\left| 80i \\right. & \\left. 80 \\right| & \\left| 60i \\right. & {\\left. 80 \\right|.\\#} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$
