({2^{1/2}v\_{i}v\_{j}} \\right)}{({2^{1/2}w\_{i}w\_{j}})}}} \\\\ {+ {\\sum\_{i = 1}^{2}\\left( {2a} \\right)}^{1/2}v\_{i}\\left( {2a} \\right)^{1/2}w\_{i} + a^{2}.} \\\\ \\end{array}$![Equation](Images/F000163si108.png)![Equation](Images/F000163si108a.png) This representation is important because it can generalize easily into higher dimensions. Also it will enable *Φ*![Equation](Images/F000163si109.png) to be found. Here, the kernel=< Φ(v), Φ(w)>. Both arguments within the inner product are the same, so factoring would yield Φ(v).

Accordingly, the mapping *Φ* : *R*²→*R*⁶![Equation](Images/F000163si110.png) is being employed in this example. The feature map *Φ*![Equation](Images/F000163si111.png) employs the two tuples of *v* = (*v*[1]*v*[2])![Equation](Images/F000163si112.png)′, in *R*²![Equation](Images/F000163si113.png). It maps them into all possible second, d=2, degree nonhomogeneous monomials, resulting in *Φ*(*v*) = (*v*[1]²*v*[1]²2^(1/2)*v*[1]*v*[2](2*a*)^(1/2)*v*[1](2*a*)^(1/2)*v*[2]*a*)![Equation](Images/F000163si114.png)′. Note here that commutativity does not matter. However, by using the same protocol as in the homogeneous case, then the mapping is *Φ* : *R*²→*R*⁷![Equation](Images/F000163si115.png), where distinct labeling does matter, that is, even though *v*[1]*v*[2] = *v*[2]*v*[1]![Equation](Images/F000163si116.png), each one occupies a distinct tuple. Thus: *Φ*(*v*) = (*v*[1]²*v*[1]²*v*[1]*v*[2]*v*[2]*v*[1](2*a*)^(1/2)*v*[1](2*a*)^(1/2)*v*[2]*a*)![Equation](Images/F000163si117.png)′.#

Recall that a kernel is a function involving a nonempty set X, such that K: X x X→R. It is linked to a map: Φ: X→H, where H is a Hilbert space over the reals. Additionally, for x and y are in X, and K defined by the inner product: K(x,y)=< Φ(x), Φ(y)>, the function Φ is called the feature map. Also, K is called the feature kernel, and H is sometimes called the feature space. H need not be a RKHS. On the other hand, a kernel in a RKHS is also a feature kernel. Feature kernels are symmetric and positive semidefinite: Let i and j be in any finite set of positive integers, and *x*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000163si118.png), *x*[*j*]![Equation](Images/F000163si119.png) in X and *a*[*i*]*a*[*j*]![Equation](Images/F000163si120.png) real valued, then ${\\sum\\limits\_{i,j}{a\_{i}a\_{j}K}}\\left( {x\_{i},x\_{j}} \\right) = {\\sum\\limits\_{i}{\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{i}a\_{j} < \\Phi\\left( x\_{i} \\right),}}}\\Phi\\left( x\_{j} \\right) > = {\\sum\\limits\_{i}{a\_{i} < \\Phi\\left( x\_{i} \\right),{\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{j}\\Phi\\left( x\_{j} \\right) > = < {\\sum\\limits\_{i}{a\_{i}\\Phi\\left( x\_{i} \\right)}},{\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{j}\\Phi\\left( x\_{j} \\right) > = \\left\\| {\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{j}\\Phi\\left( x\_{j} \\right)}} \\right\\|}}}}}}^{2}$![Equation](Images/F000163si121.png) which is greater than or equal to zero. In terms of vectors, a′ K a is greater than or equal to zero, where a is a column vector consisting of all the *a*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000163si122.png), a′ is a row vector of *a*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000163si123.png), and K is a Gram matrix.

Kernels are defined in terms of sequences in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000163si124.png). Kernel methods form a firm foundation for machine learning involving support vector-type classification. In this type of classification, hyperplanes are utilized usually in binary categorization. These planes are employed in separating two distinct data classes or objects. Indeed, these planes normally do not pass through the origin and are instances of an affine transformation. Such transformations preserve lines and keep parallels parallel. Additionally, they preserve convexity as well as extreme points. They do not preserve distance or angles. In machine learning, they are also useful because they are an automorphism of affine spaces; they preserve dimension and subspaces. The data to be categorized into two groups is first assumed to be linearly separable. This preassumes that there exists a hyperplane that can separate the data into two parts. Soft categorization is given for which the data is nonlinear separable. Soft categorization refers to the fact that data is marginally nonseparable, that is, there are occasional outliers. Also, applications of kernels in regression analysis exist. Here, parameter settings are determined that minimize overfitting or under fitting of the data by regressed curves.

Some combinations of feature maps are also feature maps. In particular, the sum and the product of feature maps is a feature map along with nonnegative scalar products. However, the difference of two feature maps might not be a feature map. These properties are used in the construction described later.

Consider a nonempty set X, and a sequence *Φ*[1]![Equation](Images/F000163si125.png), *Φ*[2]![Equation](Images/F000163si126.png), *Φ*[3]…![Equation](Images/F000163si127.png), of *l*²![Equation](Images/F000163si128.png) functions such that *Φ*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000163si129.png): X→R. Then *Φ*(*x*) = (*Φ*[1]*Φ*[2]*Φ*[3]…)![Equation](Images/F000163si130.png) is the feature map, and $K\\left( {x,y} \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}}\\Phi\_{i}\\left( x \\right)\\Phi\_{i}\\left( y \\right)$![Equation](Images/F000163si131.png) is a kernel on X. This follows using the CBS inequality, that is, $\\left| K\\left( {x,y} \\right) \\middle| = \\middle| \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}}\\Phi\_{i}\\left( x \\right)\\Phi\_{i}\\left( y \\right) \\right|$![Equation](Images/F000163si132.png) is less than or equal to $\\left. \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| \\Phi\_{i}\\left( x \\right)|^{2}\\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| \\Phi\_{i}\\left( y \\right)|^{2} \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000163si133.png).

Hyperplane A will be described herein in finite real inner product spaces *H* = *R*^(*n*)![Equation](Images/F000163si134.png). These planes will be an affine subset of H of degree less than n. For b in R, and for w in H, A={v in H, such that <w, v>+b=0}.

 

### Example 18.10

Let *H* = *R*²![Equation](Images/F000163si135.png), for b=2, and w=(1 4)′ in H, *A* = {*v*\=(*v*[1]*v*[2])![Equation](Images/F000163si136.png)′ in H, such that  < (14)′, (*v*[1]*v*[2])′>+2=0}![Equation](Images/F000163si137.png). Accordingly, A is the straight affine line: *v*[1] + 4*v*[2] =  − 2![Equation](Images/F000163si138.png).#

Support vector machine is supervised learning and needs training data. The kernel trick transforms data to a higher dimension, performs classification, and then transforms back. Points in space have tuples that are called features. The hyperplane partitions H into two half planes: *A*^+![Equation](Images/F000163si139.png)\={v in H|<w, v>+b greater than or equal to 0} and *A*^−![Equation](Images/F000163si140.png)\={v in H|<w, v>+b <0}, thus giving the hyperplane the decision boundary for binary classification. H is a metric space because it is an inner product space and therefore it is also a normed vector space. Indeed, the inner product provides a natural metric d. The distance between v and w in H is *d*(*v*,*w*) =  < *v* − *w*, *v* − *w*\>^(1/2) = ∥*v* − *w*∥![Equation](Images/F000163si141.png). The last quantity is the norm induced by the inner product. For a set of vectors, *X* = {*v*[1], *v*[2], …, *v*[*n*]}![Equation](Images/F000163si142.png) in H, the distance from a single point *v*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000163si143.png) in this set to the affine classifier A is given by | < *w*, *v*[*i*] >  + *b*|/∥*w*∥![Equation](Images/F000163si144.png). This smallest distance from a vector in X to A is given by minimizing this expression. Multiplying an affine space by constant, that is, multiplying w and b by the same constant, does not change the space A; actually the two spaces are equivalent. Thus the minimum distance can be found by min (|<*w*,*v*[*i*]\>+*b*|)![Equation](Images/F000163si145.png) for i=1, 2, …, n. See Section 2.9, involving affine spaces.

 

### Example 18.11

As in the previous example, a hyperplane will be created. Then the distance will be found from A to the closest vector in the set X. Again, let *H* = *R*²![Equation](Images/F000163si146.png), with bias b=3, and w=(1 2)′ in H, *A* = {*v*\=(*v*[1]*v*[2])![Equation](Images/F000163si147.png)′ in H, such that <(1 2)′, (*v*[1]*v*[2])![Equation](Images/F000163si148.png)′>+3=0}. Consider the set X={(0 0)′, (2 3)′, (−2–4)′}. The hyperspace line is *v*[1] + 2*v*[2] =  − 3![Equation](Images/F000163si149.png). The distance from (0 0)′ to A is|<w, (0 0)′>+b|/‖w‖=|0+3|/5^(1/2)\=3/5^(1/2).

The distance from (2 3)′ to A is|<w, (2 3)′>+b|/‖w‖=|8+3|/ 5^(1/2)\=11 / 5^(1/2).

The distance from (−2–4)′ to A is|<w, (−2–4)′>+b|/‖w‖=|−10+3|/ 5^(1/2)\=7 / 5^(1/2). Classification of all the points in X yields the following: (0 0)′ and (2 3)′ are in *A*^+![Equation](Images/F000163si150.png); also (−2–4)′ is in *A*^−![Equation](Images/F000163si151.png). In any case, the zero vector is the closest. Remembering that an affine space can be scaled, and so, multiplying by the absolute norm value of the weight w, the distance formulation is normalized, and the distances become 3, 11, and 5, respectively. By knowing the minimum distance, further scaling could be employed. Indeed, a scaling by 3‖w‖would normalize the results.#

 

## 18.10 Radial basis function kernel

Radial basis function (RBF) kernel uses, for instance, v=(x y)′ in *R*²![Equation](Images/F000163si152.png), and the mapping *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000163si153.png)(v) provides an infinite-dimensional vector *Φ*(*v*) = (1*x* *y* *x**y* *y**x* *x*²*y*²*x*²*y**y*²*x*…)![Equation](Images/F000163si154.png)′. The kernel method avoids calculating *Φ*![Equation](Images/F000163si155.png)(v), which produces the single, the double, the triple interactions, etc., between the tuples of v. Instead the inner product is performed in R², and then the kernel: *k*(*v*,*w*) =  < *Φ*(*v*), *Φ*(*w*) >  = *e*^( − 1/2*∥**v* − *w**|*|²)![Equation](Images/F000163si156.png). To show formally that this is an inner product kernel, write *e*^( − 1/2*∥**v* − *w**|*|²) = *e*^( − 1/2\[(*v* − *w*)^′(*v* − *w*)\]) = *e*^( − 1/2\[*v*^′*v* − 2*v*^′*w* + *w*^′*w*\]) = *e*^( − 1/2\[*v*^′*v* + *w*^′*w*\])*e*^(*v*^′*w*)![Equation](Images/F000163si157.png). Let *C* = *e*^( − 1/2\[*v*^′*v* + *w*^′*w*\])![Equation](Images/F000163si158.png). Then *e*^( − 1/2*∥**v* − *w**|*|²) = *C**e*^(*v*^′*w*) = *C**e*^(*v*^′*w* + 1)*e*^( − 1) = *C*′*e*^(*v*^′*w* + 1)![Equation](Images/F000163si159.png) where C′ is a new constant. Thus $e^{- 1/2{\\|{v - w}\\|}^{2}} = \\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}{\\left( {1 + \\left. {v'w} \\right\\}} \\right.^{n}/n!}$![Equation](Images/F000163si160.png) This shows that the RBF kernel makes all nonhomogeneous polynomial kernels. This kernel projects into infinite-dimensional space. It performs an infinite number of interactions between data.

The RBF model is founded on using the distance between points in space. If data consists of the pair (x[*n*], y[*n*]), this influences h(x) based on ‖x−x[*n*]‖. The standard form is $h\\left( x \\right) = \\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}{w\_{n}e^{- \\gamma{\\|{x - x\_{n}}\\|}^{2}}}$![Equation](Images/F000163si161.png). The expression is a functional form for a hypothesis. In most cases, the objective is to find w consisting of tuples w[*n*], n=1, 2,… N, based on data D=(x[*n*], y[*n*]). To solve for $w:\\overset{N}{\\underset{n = 1}{\\sum^{}}}w\_{n}e^{- \\gamma||x - x\_{n}||^{2}} = y\_{m}$![Equation](Images/F000163si162.png) for *x* = *x*[*m*]![Equation](Images/F000163si163.png)′. So *Φ*![Equation](Images/F000163si164.png) w=y. The solution is *w* = *Φ*^( − 1)*y*![Equation](Images/F000163si165.png), similar to regression. For classification, use $h\\left( x \\right) = {sgn}{({\\overset{N}{\\underset{n = 1}{\\sum^{}}}w\_{n}e^{- \\gamma||x - x\_{n}||^{2}}})}$![Equation](Images/F000163si166.png). Let $s = \\overset{N}{\\underset{n = 1}{\\sum^{}}}w\_{n}e^{- \\gamma||x - x\_{n}||^{2}}$![Equation](Images/F000163si167.png).

 

## 18.11 Bound matrices

Similar to time-limited signals described in Section 1.9, two-dimensional time-limited matrices form an inner product space ([Alotto et al., 1998](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib19); [Dougherty and Giardina, 1987](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib20)). These are real-valued functions f with finite support in *R*^(*Z**x**Z*)![Equation](Images/F000163si168.png). This is the carrier set corresponding to VECTOR, and for SCALAR, the reals are employed. The function f in *R*^(*Z**x**Z*)![Equation](Images/F000163si169.png) means that f: Z x Z→R, but all these functions described by bound matrices have nonzero values on a finite subset of lattice points. They will be denoted by A. Note that V-ZERO corresponds to the 0 entity in A. Signals or functions in A form a real-valued vector space using point-wise operations. As in the referenced section, A also forms an inner product space, using the dot product on the intersection of these matrices, but again, it is not a Hilbert space. Additionally, the cozero set, complement of zero, for f in A, is denoted by COZ(f). This finite set consists of all lattice points, (n, m) in Z x Z where f (n, m) differs from V-ZERO.

A convenient representation for any signal f in A, such that COZ(f) is not empty, is described similar to the Young diagrams in Section 15.7. Indeed, a critical lattice point (p, q) is the location of the leftmost, uppermost element of any matrix enclosing all nonzero values of f. For instance, find the point (p, q) equaling the smallest value n, for which f (n, ·) that is nonzero is located, and also the largest value of m such that f (·, m) that is nonzero is located. Next, a matrix-type structure is employed to enclose all the nonzero values of f, along with (p, q). The latter point itself might be zero. This is similar to a minimal enclosing rectangle, although the matrix need not be minimal. However, in general, there has to be at least one nonzero value in the matrix and no nonzero values outside. Once the leftmost coordinate p and uppermost value coordinate q are located, the value (p, q) is used as a pointer on the lower right-hand side of the matrix. This data structure is called a bound matrix. Throughout, it is at least initially assumed that the cozero set is nonempty. An example might be helpful.

 

### Example 18.12

Consider the two-dimensional digital signal f in A, where f is zero except on COZ(f)={(0, 0), (−1, 1), (1, 2), (1, 0), (1, 1)}. Also say that f (0, 0)=5, f (−1, 1)=3, f (1, 2)=2, f (1, 0)= −3, and finally, f (1, 1)=6. The first x coordinate set of COZ(f) consists of points in Z, which is {0, −1, 1}, and the minimum is p=−1. The second y coordinate set is {0, 1, 2}; the maximum is q=2. Accordingly, two bound matrix structures representing the function f are given by:

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 0 & {2|} \\\\ {|3} & 0 & {6|} \\\\ {|0} & 5 & {{- 3}|}\_{- 1,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & 0 & 3 & 0 & 6 & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & 0 & 0 & 5 & {- 3} & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & {0|}\_{- 3,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\operatorname{.\\#}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si170.png)

Thus it is seen that there exists an equivalence class of bound matrices representing a function in A, but this direction will not be pursued. However, in the aforementioned example, a form of compression is illustrated. The bound matrix to the left is called a minimal bound matrix, since no smaller matrix than this three-by-three matrix can capture all the nonzero values of f.

The inner product space A also forms an algebra. For f and g in A, the point-wise multiplication is the convolution defined by

BINE(f, g)(n,m)=(f⋆![Equation](Images/F000163si171.png)g)(n,m)=$\\sum\_{k = - \\infty}^{\\infty}{\\sum\_{j = - \\infty}^{\\infty}{g\\left( {n - k,m - j} \\right)f\\left( {k,j} \\right)}}$![Equation](Images/F000163si172.png). With this type of multiplication BINE, A becomes a unital, commutative, associative algebra. The unital function V-ONE is *I* = (1)[(0, 0)]![Equation](Images/F000163si173.png), and I![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)f=f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)I=f. Although the limits in the aforementioned summation are infinite, there are only a finite number of nonzero terms. A more concise expression for the actual summation limits involves the cozero sets. In particular, COZ(f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g) is a subset of the dilation of the two sets COZ(f) and COZ(g). The dilation is given by D(COZ(f),COZ(g)). This quantity equals the union of all sets of integer pairs {(n+k, m+j)}, where (n, m) is in COZ(f) and (k, j) is in COZ(g). The convolution of f and g will be zero outside this dilated set. Thus the dilation provides a support region for the convolution. Therefore, the convolution can be calculated using

(*f*⋆*g*)(*n*,*m*) = ∑*f*(*n*−*k*,*m*−*j*)*g*(*k*,*j*),

![Equation](Images/F000163si174.png)

where (k, j) is in COZ(g) and (n−k, m−j) is in COZ(f). The procedure for finding (f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g)(n,m) is to first find the dilated set D(COZ(f),COZ(g)). Only if (n,m) is in this set, then use (k, j) in COZ(g); if (n−k, m−j) is in COZ(f), then multiply f(n−k, m−j) by g(k,j). This must be calculated for all possibilities, and the sum should then be taken. This result is the convolution at (n, m). Because this sum might equal zero, it shows that the dilated set might not be the cozero set for the convolution.

 

### Example 18.13

Consider the two bound matrices f and g, in A, given by minimal bound matrix structures, respectively:

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} {|0} & {1|} \\\\ {|2} & {3|}\_{0,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|2} & {0|} \\\\ {|{- 1}} & {4|}\_{1,3} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si175.png)

COZ(f)={(1, 2), (0, 1), (1, 1)} and COZ(g)={(1, 3), (1, 2), (2, 2)}. The dilation of these two sets is D(COZ(f),COZ(g))={(2, 5), (2, 4), (3, 4), (1, 4), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 3)}. This set of lattice points will only provide a support region for the convolution. Outside this region, all zeros appear at lattice points. Beginning with the first element in this set, (n, m)=(2, 5), use (k, j)=(1, 3) in COZ(g), and then see if (n−k, m−j)=(1, 2) is in COZ(f). Yes, it is, so find the product, f(1, 2)·g (1, 3)=1·2=2. Next, the second element in this set (n, m)=(2, 4), use (k, j)=(1, 3) in COZ(g), and then see if (n−k, m−j)=(1, 1) is in COZ(f). Yes, it is, so find the product, f(1, 1)·g (1, 3)=3·2=6. But (k, j)=(1, 2) also works, that is, (n−k, m−j)=(1, 2) is in COZ(f); accordingly f(1, 2)·g (1, 2)=1·(−1)=−1. These must be added together; thus (f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g)(2, 4)=6–1=5.

Next, the third element in this set (n, m)=(3, 4), use (k, j)=(1, 3) in COZ(g), and then see if (n−k, m−j)=(2, 1) is in COZ(f). No, then try (k, j)=(1, 2) in COZ(g); then see if (n−k, m−j)=(2, 2) is in COZ(f). Again no, then try (k, j)=(2, 2) in COZ(g); then see if (n−k, m−j)=(1, 2) is in COZ(f). Yes, it is, so find the product, f(1, 2)·g (2, 2)=1·4=4. Next, the fourth element in this set (n, m)=(1, 4), use (k, j)=(1, 3) in COZ(g), and then see if (n−k, m−j)=(0, 1) is in COZ(f). Yes, it is, so find the product, f(0, 1)·g (1, 3)=2·2=4. Next, the fifth element in this set (n, m)=(1, 3), use (k, j)=(1, 2) in COZ(g), and then see if (n−k, m−j)=(0, 1) is in COZ(f). Yes, it is, so find the product, f(0, 1)·g (1, 2)=2·(−1)= −2.

Next for the sixth element in the dilated set, (n, m)=(2, 3), use (k, j)=(1, 2) in COZ(g), and then see if (n−k, m−j)=(1, 1) is in COZ(f). Yes, it is, so find the product, f(1, 1)·g (1, 2)=3·−1=−3. However, (k, j)=(2, 2) also works since if (n−k, m−j)=(0, 1) is in COZ(f). Then f (0, 1)·g (2, 2)=2·4=8. Adding yields −3+8=5. Finally, the last value in the dilated set is (n, m)=(3, 3), and (k, j)=(2, 2) works because (n−k, m−j)=(1, 1) is in COZ(f). Therefore, f (1, 1)·g (2, 2)=3·4=12.

Consequently, the bound matrix for f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g is the following:

$\\begin{matrix} {|0} & 2 & {0|} \\\\ {|4} & 5 & {4|} \\\\ {|{- 2}} & 5 & {12|}\_{1,5} \\\\ \\end{matrix}\\operatorname{.\\#}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si176.png)

As in the bound vector description in Section 3.2, there exists a parallel algorithm for finding bound matrix convolution. It too is illustrated in [Figure 3.2](#Ch003_41-55_B9780443136979000175.xhtml#f0015). In short the method is

*f* ⋆ *g* = *A**D**D*\[*S**C**A**L**A**R*(*g*(*n*,*m*),*T**R**A**N*(*f*; *n*,*m*)),*f**o**r*(*n*,*m*)*i**n**C**O**Z*(*g*).![Equation](Images/F000163si177.png)

SCALAR is just multiplication of translates of the matrix for f, by values of g, located at (n, m). TRAN just translates the matrix for f by changing the location pointer on the lower right outside corner of the matrix. The change occurs by adding, resulting in (p+n, q+m). The values within the matrix do not change by only using this operation. The difference between the parallel convolution equation mentioned earlier and the referenced figure is none. SCALAR and TRAN operations commute!

 

### Example 18.14

Referring to Example 8.13 where COZ(g)={(1, 3), (1, 2), (2, 2)}, also g (1, 3)=2, g (1, 2)= −1, g (2, 2)=4. Then f is given below, followed by g (1, 3) ·TRAN(f; 1, 3), followed by an application of g(1, 2)·TRAN (f; 1, 2), finally multiplying g (2, 2)·TRAN (2, 2):

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} {|0} & {1|} \\\\ {|2} & {3|}\_{0,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & {2|} \\\\ {|4} & {6|}\_{1,5} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & {{- 1}|} \\\\ {|{- 2}} & {{- 3}|}\_{1,4} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & {4|} \\\\ {|8} & {{12|}\_{2,4}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si178.png)

Rewriting the last three bound matrices with a common location indicator gives the following:

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 2 & {0|} \\\\ {|4} & 6 & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & 0 & {0|}\_{1,5} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 0 & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & {- 1} & {0|} \\\\ {|{- 2}} & {- 3} & {0|}\_{1,5} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 0 & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & 0 & {4|} \\\\ {|0} & 8 & {{12|}\_{1,5}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si179.png)

Adding the aforementioned three bound matrices together gives exactly the same answer as previously given in [Example 18.13](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#enun13).#

A bound matrix with minimal support for f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g, where f and g are in A, can be found. Assume that the convolution is not equal to zero. First find D(COZ(f),COZ(g)). Then in this set find the minimum value of the first tuple and the maximum value of the second tuple; call this (p, q). Use this as the location of the left uppermost entry in the bound matrix for the convolution. The actual bound matrix of support is N by M where N=p′−p,+1, where p′ is the largest value of the first tuple in the dilated set, and M=q−q′+1, where q′ is the minimum value of the second tuple in the dilated set.

 

### Example 18.15

Again refer to [Example 18.13](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#enun13), where D(COZ(f),COZ(g))={(2, 5), (2, 4), (3, 4), (1, 4), (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 3)}. Then (p, q)=(1, 5), and since p′=3 and q′=3, then N=3–1+1=3, M=5–3+1=3.#

Similar to [Section 3.9](#Ch003_41-55_B9780443136979000175.xhtml#s0050), where wraparound bound vectors were described, wraparound bound matrices also form a Banach\* algebra. In this case, functions f in *R*^(*Z*[*r*]*x**Z*[*r*])![Equation](Images/F000163si180.png) are utilized. These are functions with domain {0, 1, … r−1} x {0, 1, … r−1}, with codomain the real numbers. Moreover, *Z*[*r*]![Equation](Images/F000163si181.png) has a cyclic group structure, modular r. The set of all these functions for fixed positive integer r will be denoted by *A*[*r*]![Equation](Images/F000163si182.png). Bound matrices provide a convenient representation for elements in *A*[*r*]![Equation](Images/F000163si183.png). Point-wise addition, scalar multiplication, and so on show that this structure becomes a real-valued vector space with V-ZERO being the bound matrix of all zeros. Additionally, convolutional multiplication gives a structure of a unital, abelian, and associative algebra. The unity element, V-ONE, is a bound matrix of all zeros, except that at the (0, 0) location there is a one. Finally, a Hilbert space structure is created using the *l*²![Equation](Images/F000163si184.png) norm. The completeness follows as in Appendix A.1.

Just like the one-dimensional case of wraparound bound vectors, a superscript (*W*[*r*]) will appear on the upper right-hand corner for modulo r bound matrices. It also indicates an *r*²![Equation](Images/F000163si185.png) size of bound matrix is being utilized. Additionally, a subscript outside the lower right-hand side indicates the upper left-hand entry of the wraparound bound matrix. An example should help make some of these concepts more understandable.

 

### Example 18.16

Consider the wraparound bound matrix, f in *A*[3]![Equation](Images/F000163si186.png); it is given below as described earlier. This is followed below by the scalar multiple of f by 2, that is, SCALAR(f; 2). Finally, the third matrix below is a more compact representation for this actually three-by-three matrix:#

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & 2 & {- 1} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right|^{W3} \\\\ \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & {- 3} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right| \\\\ \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right|\_{0,3} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & 4 & {- 2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right|^{W3} \\\\ \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & {- 6} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right| \\\\ \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right|\_{0,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} \\left| \\begin{matrix} 2 & {- 1} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right|^{W3} \\\\ \\left| \\begin{matrix} 0 & {- 3} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\right|\_{1,3} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si187.png)

Additionally, the two norm of f is ∥*f*∥[2] = (4+1+9)^(1/2) = 14^(1/2)![Equation](Images/F000163si188.png), whereas the one norm is ∥*f*∥[1] = 6![Equation](Images/F000163si189.png).#

The cozero set for f in *A*[*r*]![Equation](Images/F000163si190.png) consists of {(n, m) in *Z*[*r*]*x**Z*[*r*]![Equation](Images/F000163si191.png) such that f (n, m) in R−{0}}. As before, the dilated set for two functions in *A*[*r*]![Equation](Images/F000163si192.png) is of the uttermost importance in calculating the convolution. The dilated set is a support region for the convolution, and consequently only points within this set should be employed for this operation. The convolution can be calculated using:

(*f*⋆*g*)(*n*,*m*) = ∑*f*(*n*−*k*,*m*−*j*)*g*(*k*,*j*),

![Equation](Images/F000163si193.png)

where (k, j) is in COZ(g) and (n−k, m−j) is in COZ(f). The procedure for finding (f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g)(n,m) is, as before, to first find the dilated set D(COZ(f),COZ(g)). Only if (n,m) is in this set, then use (k, j) in COZ(g); if (n−k, m−j) is in COZ(f), then multiply f(n−k, m−j) by g(k,j). This must be calculated for all possibilities, and the sum should then be taken. This result is the convolution at (n, m). Before an example is provided, it is best to introduce the parallel algorithm.

The parallel algorithm for finding wraparound bound matrix convolution is illustrated in [Figure 3.2](#Ch003_41-55_B9780443136979000175.xhtml#f0015). As before, the method is:

*f* ⋆ *g* = *A**D**D*\[*S**C**A**L**A**R*(*g*(*n*,*m*),*T**R**A**N*(*f*; *n*,*m*)),*f**o**r*(*n*,*m*)*i**n**C**O**Z*(*g*).![Equation](Images/F000163si194.png)

Again, SCALAR, in this formula, is multiplication of translates of the matrix for f. The multiplication factor is the value of g, located at (n, m). This is similar to the multiplication in the bound matrix situation. TRAN just translates the matrix for f by changing the location pointer on the lower right outside corner of the matrix, but this is performed modulo r. The change occurs by adding. Resulting in (p+n, q+m), all operations modulo r. The values within the matrix do not change with only this operation.

 

### Example 18.17

Again consider the wraparound function f in *A*[3]![Equation](Images/F000163si195.png) from the previous example. It is given again below followed by g also in *A*[3]![Equation](Images/F000163si196.png). The objective is to find f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g. The operation will be performed using the parallel algorithm, and then a value or two will be checked using the point-wise calculation.

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} {|2} & {{- 1}|}^{W3} \\\\ {|0} & {{- 3}|}\_{1,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|1} & {4|}^{W3} \\\\ {|0} & {{5|}\_{1,2}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si197.png)

First finding the cozero sets, COZ (f)={(1, 2), (2, 2), (2, 1)}, and COZ (g)={(1, 2), (2, 2), (2, 1)}. The dilation is D(COZ (f), COZ (g))={(2, 4), (3, 4), (3, 3), (4, 4), (4, 3), (4, 2)}={(2, 1), (0, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1), (1, 0), (1, 2)}. The last set of integer pairs occurs since all domain operations are performed modulo three. Reading off the values for matrix g gives g (1, 2)=1, g (2, 2)=4, g (2, 1)=5. Preparing for the parallel algorithm, first f is given below. This is followed by g (1, 2) ·TRAN(f; 1, 2). Next, it follows g(2, 2)·TRAN (f; 2, 2). Finally, use g (2, 1)·TRAN (f; 2, 1).

$\\begin{matrix} {|\\begin{matrix} 2 & {- 1} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}^{W3} & {|\\begin{matrix} 2 & {- 1} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}^{W3} & {|\\begin{matrix} 8 & {- 4} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}^{W3} & {|\\begin{matrix} 10 & {- 5} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}^{W3} \\\\ {|\\begin{matrix} 0 & {- 3} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}\_{1,2} & {|\\begin{matrix} 0 & {- 3} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}\_{2,1} & {|\\begin{matrix} 0 & {- 12} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}\_{0,1} & {{|\\begin{matrix} 0 & {- 15} \\\\ \\end{matrix}|}\_{0,0}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si198.png)

Rewriting the last three matrices with a common pointer gives:

$\\begin{matrix} \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 0 & {0|}^{W3} \\\\ {|{- 1}} & 0 & {2|} \\\\ {|{- 3}} & 0 & {0|}\_{0,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & 0 & {0|}^{W3} \\\\ {|8} & {- 4} & {0|} \\\\ {|0} & {- 12} & {0|}\_{0,2} \\\\ \\end{matrix} & \\begin{matrix} {|0} & {- 15} & {0|}^{W3} \\\\ {|0} & 0 & {0|} \\\\ {|10} & {- 5} & {{0|}\_{0,2}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si199.png)

Adding these is simple compared with the earlier, more compact representation. As a consequence, the result is f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g.=

$\\begin{matrix} {|0} & {- 15} & {0|}^{W3} \\\\ {|7} & {- 4} & {2|} \\\\ {|7} & {- 17} & {{0|}\_{0,2}.} \\\\ \\end{matrix}$

![Equation](Images/F000163si200.png)

As a check, consider f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g (0, 0)=f (1, 2)·g (2, 1)+f (2, 1)·g (1, 2)=2·5+(−3) ·1=7. Also f![ent](Images/sstarf_8902.png)g (0, 1)=f (1, 2)·g (2, 2)+f (2, 2)·g (1, 2)=2·4+(−1)·1=7.#

 

## 18.12 Convolutional neural networks and quantum convolutional neural networks

The principal operation in a convolutional neural network (CNN) is convolution. This operation is often performed at several layers in a CNN architecture. [Fig. 18.4](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#f0025) provides a typical illustration of the operations within a CNN used in imaging. Very often, in between convolution operations, some type of compression is performed. These operations are illustrated in the figure and are called pooling layers. In these operations, a small number of pixels, usually in a rectangular pattern, are converted into to a single scalar value. This is often done by max pooling, wherein the largest value among all the pixel values is chosen as the representative. Sometimes, the average or median value is calculated and employed. In any case, a source coding has occurred, and the result is a reduced computational burden. The final operation is a typical fully connected NN layer. Often backpropagation is performed to adjust critical parameters involving the convolutional kernels. Convolutional kernels in the past were often handcrafted. However, with the back end NN being utilized often, more useful kernels can be machine learned.

![Figure 18.4 Convolutional neural network.](Images/F000163f18-04-9780443136979.jpg)

[Figure 18.4](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#Bf0025) Convolutional neural network.

In the referenced figure, C represents a convolutional layer. The leftmost convolutional layer, for instance, might seek out edges or low-level characterization of texture. Adjacent to C is P representing a pooling layer. This layer might reduce the noise level. The next convolutional layer might be used for recognizing more complex structures. The last layer is often a fully connected NN.

In CNN, there exists an observed image f, for instance, consisting of N by M pixels represented by a bound matrix. The convolution process involves a heuristically determined smaller n by m bound matrix g, called the kernel that is convolved with f. The observed image in this case is said to be filtered by g. Usually, the filtering matrix is required to fit into the interior of the observed image. Because of this arrangement, the resulting convolution is of dimensions N−n+1 by M−m+1. To prevent shrinkage, often the observed image is enlarged by adding a boarder.

Recently, there has been a surge of papers and articles on quantum versions of CNN, QCNN ([Hur et al., 2022](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib6)). They are used in classical machine learning classification contexts and exploit entanglement. QCNNs are also employed in conventional image processing applications such as spatial filtering, edge detection, as well as handwritten symbol recognition ([Wei et al., 2022](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib14)). As in the past, research continues using machine learning devices to classify high-energy events in physics. An instance of this research is the article [Chen et al., (2022)](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib3). Another instance of this type of application can be found in [Hermann et al. (2022)](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib5). In this report, QCNNs are utilized on a superconducting quantum processor for recognizing quantum phases. Some papers explain how QCNNs can be implemented using quantum circuits ([Zheng et al., 2022](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib17)). In this article, a universal QCNN model is proposed consisting of all three: the convolutional layer, the pooling layer, and a fully connected NN layer. Several papers have emerged on medical-type applications using QCNNs ([Magallanes et al., 2022](#Ch018_327-348_B9780443136979000163.xhtml#bib8)).

 Chapter 19 

# Reproducing kernel and other Hilbert spaces

 

## Abstract

The chapter begins with an algebraic solution to the harmonic oscillator. The key to the solution is the creation ladder operator cyclic property. This leads to the Hermite polynomial solution. Section 19.2 begins the description of the reproducing Hilbert space over the complex field. The Hardy disk algebra is also introduced in this section, as well as the Bargmann kernel and the Jordan algebra. The following section illustrates the reproducing Hilbert space over the real field. The next section is dedicated to Mercer’s theorem along with examples of Fredholm-type integral equations of the second kind. The spectral theorem involving projective-valued measures is described in the next section. Following this is the Riesz-Markov theorem. The next section provides examples of nonseparable Hilbert spaces. In particular, the nonseparable Hilbert space of almost periodic functions is illustrated. The chapter ends with proof that all separable Hilbert spaces are isometrically isomorphic To l².

 

### Keywords

Disk algebra; Hardy space; Mittag-Leffler function; Jordon algebra; Bargmann-Fock space; Mercer’s theorem; Riesz-Markov theorem; band-limited functions; Szego kernel; Siegal-Bergman kernel

 

## 19.1 Algebraic solution to harmonic oscillator

In [Section 6.1](#Ch006_103-128_B9780443136979000217.xhtml#s0010), the ground-state solution to the harmonic oscillator is shown to be equal to *Ψ*[0] = (*m* *w*[0]/(*π**h*))^(1/4)*e*^( − *m**w*[0]*x*²/(2*h*))![Equation](Images/F000278si1.png). The solution was obtained by solving a first-order differential equation and normalizing a Gaussian-type kernel. The normalization involved finding N=(m w[0]/(*π* h))^(1/4). For the general quantum harmonic oscillator, the time-independent Schrodinger equation is as follows:  − *h*²/(2*m*)∂²*Ψ*(*x*)/∂*x*∂*x* + 1/2*m**w*[0]²*x*²*Ψ*(*x*) = *E**Ψ*(*x*)![Equation](Images/F000278si2.png). The objective is to find the allowed energy states E, as eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions, *Ψ*![Equation](Images/F000278si3.png) (x). These functions should be normalized and either symmetric or antisymmetric about x=0. Moreover, the probability density function, |*Ψ*(*x*)|²![Equation](Images/F000278si4.png), must be finite over the interval (−∞, ∞).

Following the excellent presentation provided in [Hall (2013)](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib5), the solutions for higher energy, that is, the solutions for excited state levels, will be found in a purely algebraic manner. In the referenced text, one can find important domain issues concerning the unbounded creation and annihilation operators used in this development. From an algebraic viewpoint, the key identities involve the ground state, *Ψ*[0]![Equation](Images/F000278si5.png). First, using the annihilation operation a yields a |*Ψ*[0] >  = 0![Equation](Images/F000278si6.png). Second, there exist cyclic properties for the creation operation *a*^†:(*a*^†)^(*n*)|*Ψ*[0] >  = *Ψ*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000278si7.png), where n is a nonnegative integer. See [Section 15.2](#Ch015_271-288_B9780443136979000291.xhtml#s0015) for details on the cyclic property of a^†. A result of the cyclic property is that the excited state *Ψ*[*n*] = *H*[*n*]*Ψ*[0]![Equation](Images/F000278si8.png). Here, *H*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000278si9.png) is a polynomial of degree n, and it can be found using induction, starting with *H*[0] = 1![Equation](Images/F000278si10.png). Additionally, these polynomials are called the Hermite polynomials. They are orthogonal on (−∞, ∞), a consequence of being solutions to a Sturm-Liouville differential equation. See Appendix A.7. Using the Rodrigues formula for Hermite polynomials: *H*[*n*] = (−1)^(*n*)*e*^(*x*²)*d*^(*n*)*e*^( − *x*²)/*d**x*^(*n*)![Equation](Images/F000278si11.png), n=0, 1, 2, … gives, for instance, H[0]\=1, H[1]\=2 x, H[2]\=4 x²–2, and H[3]\=8 x³–12 x, …

Accordingly, the wave function solutions are *Ψ*[*n*] = *N* *H*[*n*](*b* *x*)*e*^( − (*b**x*)²/2)![Equation](Images/F000278si12.png), where *b* = \[(*m**w*[0])/*h*\]^(1/2)![Equation](Images/F000278si13.png). These solutions have corresponding eigenvalues given by allowable discrete energy levels *E*[*n*] = (2*n*+1)*h* *w*[0]/2, *n* = 0, 1, 2, ….![Equation](Images/F000278si14.png) [Fig. 19.1](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#f0010) illustrates the even symmetry for even-numbered wave functions and odd symmetry for the odd-numbered wave functions. Moreover, when the horizontal coordinate is zero, there is either an extreme point or a zero crossing for each wave function. The zero crossings occur mod2, starting with Ψ[0], and local maxima occur mod4, and so do the local minima.

![Figure 19.1 The first five wave functions for the harmonic oscillator.](Images/F000278f19-01-9780443136979.jpg)

[Figure 19.1](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#Bf0010) The first five wave functions for the harmonic oscillator.

 

## 19.2 Reproducing kernel Hilbert space over C and the disk algebra

To begin, a useful and intuitive definition of H being a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) over X means that H is a Hilbert space of complex-valued continuous functions over the nonempty set X. So, H is a subset of *C*^(*X*)![Equation](Images/F000278si15.png). Also, for all functions or vectors, f and g in H, and *ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000278si16.png)\> 0, there exists a *δ*![Equation](Images/F000278si17.png)\> 0, such that if ‖f−g‖<*δ*![Equation](Images/F000278si18.png), then |f(x)−g(x)|<*ϵ*![Equation](Images/F000278si19.png). Accordingly, this means that the functions are point-wise continuous. Using RKHS, boundedness and continuity are not related. To see that this is a subtle requirement, consider the following illustration.

 

### Example 19.1

Let H be the Hilbert space of complex-valued absolute squared functions, on \[0, 1\]. Consider the two functions f=t on this closed interval and g=t on \[0, 1) and g(1)=4 + 3i. In this case, ‖f−g‖=0; however, sup |f−g|=5. These functions are bounded, but not continuous.#

In the previous example, it was shown that boundedness in the Hilbert space plays no role in point-wise calculations as far as continuity is concerned. A function K: X²→C is called a reproducing kernel of H, whenever H contains all unary functions for x in X, where K[*x*] (y)=K (x, y), and for every x in X and f in H, then f (x)=<f, K[*x*]\>. The last property is the actual reproducing property.

The key to a rigorous approach for creating a RKHS and relating it to the reproducing property is the Riesz representation theorem (RRT): For a Hilbert space H, with inner product <·,·>: H x H→C and any continuous linear functional *ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000278si20.png) in H\*, there exists a unique vector *f*[*ϕ*]![Equation](Images/F000278si21.png) in H such that *ϕ*(*v*) =  < *v*, *f*[*ϕ*]\>![Equation](Images/F000278si22.png), for all v in H. Additionally, the norms are equal, that is, ∥*f*[*ϕ*]∥ = ∥*ϕ*∥![Equation](Images/F000278si23.png). The first norm is in H, and the second norm is in H\*, where‖*ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000278si24.png)‖=inf {C> 0 such that |*ϕ*![Equation](Images/F000278si25.png) (v)|<C‖v‖ for all v in H}.

Getting back to the RKHS, there is a linear evaluation functional *E*[*x*]:*H*→*C*![Equation](Images/F000278si26.png) (or R in the next section), such that *E*[*x*](*f*) = *f*(*x*)![Equation](Images/F000278si27.png) is bounded. By the RRT, every bounded linear functional is given by an inner product with a unique vector in H; thus for every x in X, there is a unique function *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si28.png) in H such that for all g in H, *g*(*x*) =  < *g*, *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si29.png)\>. Following [Putnam (2019)](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib9), *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si30.png) is called the reproducing kernel at the point x. The reproducing kernel for H is K: X x X→H, and it is defined by *K*(*x*,*y*) =  < *k*[*y*], *k*[*x*]\>![Equation](Images/F000278si31.png). Also, |*E*[*x*]|² =  < *k*[*x*], *k*[*x*] >  = ∥*k*[*x*]∥² = *K*(*x*,*x*)![Equation](Images/F000278si32.png). So a reproducing Hilbert space H, over C, contains a reproducing kernel K, having the reproducing property, <K(., x), f>=f(x), for all x in X and f in H. Additionally, if there exists a reproducing kernel, then H is a RKHS. That is, the linear evaluation function *E*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si33.png) is bounded. Here, *E*[*x*](*f*) =  < *K*(.,*x*), *f* >  = *f*(*x*)![Equation](Images/F000278si34.png), and so by the CBS inequality, it follows that |*E*[*x*](*f*)|![Equation](Images/F000278si35.png) is less than or equal to ∥*K*(.,*x*)∥∥*f*∥ =  < *K*(.,*x*), *K*(.,*x*\>^(1/2)∥*f*∥ = *K*(*x*,*x*)^(1/2)![Equation](Images/F000278si36.png)‖f‖, and so *E*[*x*](*f*)![Equation](Images/F000278si37.png) is bounded and |*E*[*x*]|![Equation](Images/F000278si38.png) is less than or equal to *K*(*x*,*x*)^(1/2)![Equation](Images/F000278si39.png).

The kernel is self-reproducing and positive semidefinite. Use <K(., x), K(., y)>=K(y, x)=<K(., y), K(., x)>\*. To see that the property, positive semidefiniteness holds, let i and j be in any finite set of positive integers. Then $\\left. \\left. {\\sum\\limits\_{i,j}a\_{i}^{\*}}a\_{j}K{({x\_{i},x\_{j}})} = {\\sum\\limits\_{i}a\_{i}^{\*}} < K\\left( {.,x\_{i}} \\right),{\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{j}K{({.,x\_{j}})} > = < {\\sum a\_{i}^{\*}}K\\left( {.,x\_{i}} \\right)}},{\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{j}K{({.,x\_{j}})}}} > = \\right\\|{\\sum\\limits\_{j}{a\_{j}K{({.,x\_{j}})}}} \\middle| |^{2} \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000278si40.png) which is greater than or equal to zero. This holds for all *a*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000278si41.png) in C and *x*[*i*]![Equation](Images/F000278si42.png) in X. Kernels having these properties are sometimes called Mercer kernels. There is a converse to this result. It says whenever a symmetric positive semidefinite kernel K on a set X exists, then there is a unique Hilbert space H for which K produces a RKHS. This theorem is due to Moore-Aronszajn ([Aronszajn, 1950](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib1)). An outline of the results from this paper follows. For any x in X, let K(x,.) be an operator *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si43.png). Define the set of all *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si44.png) as a, the linear span for a vector space comprised of all linear combinations of such operators over C. An inner product can be defined for two such linear combinations as $< \\overset{n}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{i}K\_{xi},\\overset{m}{\\underset{j = 1}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{j}K\_{yj} > = \\overset{n}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}}\\overset{m}{\\underset{j = 1}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{j}a\_{i}^{\*}K(x\_{i},x\_{j})$![Equation](Images/F000278si45.png). The properties of an inner product hold since the kernel is symmetric and positive definite. Let H be the completion of this inner product space. This shows that H consists of functions $f(x) = \\overset{n}{\\underset{i = 1}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{i}K\_{xi}(x)$![Equation](Images/F000278si46.png) such that the limit supremum as n goes to infinity and positive nonzero m> n, $\\left\\| \\overset{n + m}{\\underset{i = n}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{i}K\_{xi} \\right\\| = 0$![Equation](Images/F000278si47.png).

To see that the reproducing property holds, <f, $K\_{x} > = < \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}{a\_{i}K\_{xi}\\left( x \\right),K\_{x} > = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}{a\_{i} < K\_{xi},K\_{x} > = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}{a\_{i}K\\left( {x\_{xi},x} \\right) = f\\left( x \\right)}}}$![Equation](Images/F000278si48.png). In order to determine that the Hilbert space is unique, let H! be another Hilbert space of functions having K as a reproducing kernel; then for every x and y in X, this other Hilbert space would have inner product  < *K*[*x**i*]![Equation](Images/F000278si49.png), *K*[*x*]\>![Equation](Images/F000278si50.png), which again is *K*(*x*[*x**i*],*x*)![Equation](Images/F000278si51.png). Using linearity, both inner products are the same on the span using all *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si52.png). Also assume that the completion is performed as before, but for H!. This shows that H is a closed subset of H!. To prove that the inclusion goes the other way, use f in H!, and write *f* = *f*[*H*] + *f*[*H*]^⊥![Equation](Images/F000278si53.png), where *f*[*H*]![Equation](Images/F000278si54.png) is in H and *f*[*H*]^⊥![Equation](Images/F000278si55.png) is in *H*^⊥![Equation](Images/F000278si56.png). Because K is the reproducing kernel for both H and H!, it follows using inner products in H! that *f*(*x*) =  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si57.png), *f* >  =  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si58.png), *f*[*H*] >  +  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si59.png), *f*[*H*]^⊥ >  =  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si60.png), *f*[*H*]\>![Equation](Images/F000278si61.png). Because,  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si62.png), *f*[*H*]^⊥![Equation](Images/F000278si63.png)\>=0 and since *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si64.png) is in H, it follows that the inner product of *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si65.png) with *f*[*H*]^⊥![Equation](Images/F000278si66.png) in H! is zero. Therefore, the inner product in H! equals the inner product in H, showing that  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si67.png), *f*[*H*] >  = *f*[*H*]![Equation](Images/F000278si68.png), and so H=H!.

If H is the space of functions from X to C, then a functional on this space can be found for x in X; write *E*[*x*]*f* = *f*(*x*)![Equation](Images/F000278si69.png). Given a set X, a RKHS H is the space of functions from X to C; the evaluation functionals for each x in X, *E*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si70.png): H→C, are bounded, as originally stated.

 

### Example 19.2

The Hardy space is a Hilbert space, *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si71.png); it consists of all analytic functions f, on the open unit disk, D in C. The mean square value of these functions on any circle of radius r is bounded as r approaches one from the interior. That is, ∥*f*||²\=sup\[1/(2*π*)∫[0]^(2*π*)|*f*(*r**e*^(*i**θ*)|²*d**θ*\]<∞![Equation](Images/F000278si72.png), where the supremum is taken over all 0 <r <1 ([Katznelson, 1976](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib7)). As a result of Fatou’s theorem ([Krantz, 2007](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib8)), the analytic function can be extended to a function in *L*²![Equation](Images/F000278si73.png) on the boundary of the disk. It becomes the point-wise limit almost everywhere. The limit is always taken from the interior and never a tangential limit. Also, using the uniform norm for f, that is,‖f‖=max {f (z) such that z is in clos(D)}, *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si74.png) is a commutative Banach algebra. For f(z) in *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si75.png), $f\\left( z \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{n}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si76.png) analytic in unit disk D, and such that $\\left. \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| a\_{n}|^{2} < \\infty \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000278si77.png). This is called the disk algebra.

To construct the Hardy RKHS, let L: *H*^∞→*l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si78.png), where *L*(*f*) = (*a*[0] *a*[1]…)![Equation](Images/F000278si79.png). The Hardy space *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si80.png) is identified with *l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si81.png). Because L is linear and is an isometric isomorphism between *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si82.png) and *l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si83.png), this implies that *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si84.png) is a Hilbert space. Using the formal power series inner product, let $f\\left( z \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{n}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si85.png) and $g\\left( z \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}b\_{n}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si86.png) be analytic in the unit disk D. The inner product is $< f,g > = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{n}^{\*}b\_{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si87.png). All sums are from zero to infinity from here on. By the CBS inequality, |∑^()*a*[*k*]^(\*)*b*[*k*]|²![Equation](Images/F000278si88.png) is less than or equal to ∑|*a*[*k*]|²∑|*b*[*k*]|²![Equation](Images/F000278si89.png). So for every *z*[0]![Equation](Images/F000278si90.png) in D, *g*[*z*[*o*]](*z*) = ∑*z*[0]\*^(*n*)*z*^(*n*) = 1/(1−*z*[0]\**z*)![Equation](Images/F000278si91.png). Note that <f, *g*[*z*[*o*]] >  = ∑*a*[*k*]*z*[0]\*^(*n*) = *f*(*z*[0])![Equation](Images/F000278si92.png), and |<f, *g*[*z*[*o*]]![Equation](Images/F000278si93.png)\>| is less than or equal to ∥*f*∥∥*g*[*z*[*o*]]∥![Equation](Images/F000278si94.png). The results will lead to an evaluation functional. The induced norm is $\\left\\| f \\middle| |^{2} = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| a\_{n}|^{2} \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000278si95.png). To see that each power series converges to a function on D, simultaneously, consider the evaluation functional *E*[*z*](*f*)![Equation](Images/F000278si96.png). The objective then is to show that it is bounded, for z in D, so let $E\_{z}\\left( f \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{n}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si97.png). This is a complex number, so *E*[*z*]![Equation](Images/F000278si98.png) is a functional. The absolute value $\\left| E\_{z}\\left( f \\right) \\middle| = \\middle| \\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}{a\_{n}z^{n}} \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000278si99.png) | is less than or equal to $\\left. \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| a\_{n} \\right\\| z|^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si100.png) is less than or equal to $\\left\\lbrack \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| a\_{n}|^{2}\\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}} \\middle| z|^{2n} \\right\\rbrack^{1/2}$![Equation](Images/F000278si101.png) that is less than or equal to ‖f‖ \[1/(1−|z|²)\]^(1/2). Accordingly, ‖E[*Z*]‖ is bounded by \[1/(1−|z|²)\]^(1/2), and *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si102.png) is a RKHS over X=D. The kernel for a point w in D, in this case, is the Szego kernel: *K*(*z*,*w*) = *K*[*w*](*z*) = 1/(1+*w*\**z*)![Equation](Images/F000278si103.png). To see this, use the definition of the inner product for $g\\left( z \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}w^{n\_{\\ast}}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si104.png) and $f\\left( z \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}a\_{n}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si105.png), both in *H*^∞![Equation](Images/F000278si106.png). Here $< g,f > = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}w^{n}a\_{n} = f\\left( w \\right)$![Equation](Images/F000278si107.png). This means that g is a reproducing kernel for w in X=D, and therefore, summing the series for $g = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}w^{n\_{\\ast}}z^{n}$![Equation](Images/F000278si108.png) gives the Szego kernel K(w, z)=1/(1−w\*z). Also, ‖E[*Z*]‖²\=K(z, z)=1/(1−z\*z)=1/(1−|z|²).#

For every x in X, there is a *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si109.png) in H such that for all f in H <f, *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si110.png)\>=f(x). The function *K*(*x*,*y*) =  < *K*[*x*]![Equation](Images/F000278si111.png), *K*[*y*]![Equation](Images/F000278si112.png)\> is called the kernel function corresponding to H. K is positive definite, that is, for all finite collections of vectors v1… vj, in X the gram-type matrix is positive definite. An alternate definition of kernel function x in X, as well as a feature map *Φ*:*X*→*l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si113.png), is given by the m tuple, (*Φ*[1]…*Φ*[*m*])![Equation](Images/F000278si114.png), where ∑|*Φ*[*k*]|² < ∞![Equation](Images/F000278si115.png). In this case,  < *Φ*(*x*), *Φ*(*y*) >  = ∑*Φ*[*k*](*x*) \* *Φ*[*k*](*y*) = *K*(*x*,*y*)![Equation](Images/F000278si116.png). From H²→*Φ*[*k*](*z*) = *z*^(*k* − 1)![Equation](Images/F000278si117.png). Every kernel function can be written as a feature space.

 

### Example 19.3

For the vector space of polynomials with domain in D, here D is the unit disk in C and the closure in L² is the Hilbert space. The associated inner product for z^(*n*) and z^(*m*) analytic in D is given by  < *z*^(*n*), *z*^(*m*) >  = ∫[*D*]*z*^(*n*[\*])*z*^(*m*)*d**x**d**y* = ∫[0]^(2*π*)∫[0]¹*r*^(*n*)*e*^( − *i**n**θ*)*r*^(*m*)*e*^(*i**m**θ*)*r**d**r**d**θ*![Equation](Images/F000278si118.png). It equals zero for all m not equal to n, and when they are equal, <z^(*n*), z^(*m*)\>=*π*![Equation](Images/F000278si119.png)/(n + 1).

The Bergman kernel is K(z, u)=1/\[*π* (1−z\* u)²\], where|z|<1 and|u|<1. This follows by using power series, and all sums employ index variable going from zero to infinity. To begin, notice that K (z, u)=∑ \[1/*π* (n + 1) z^(*n*)\* u^(*n*)\] should be the reproducing kernel. Proceeding formally, consider *f*(*u*) = ∑*a**m* *u*^(*m*)![Equation](Images/F000278si120.png), analytic in D; then <K(z, u), f(u)>=<K(z, u), ∑ an u^(*m*)\>=∑ ∑an \[1/*π* (n + 1) <z^(*n*)\* u^(*n*), u^(*m*)\>\]=∑ ∑an \[1/*π* (n + 1) z^(*n*) <u^(*n*), u^(*m*)\>\]=∑an z^(*n*)\=f (z). Since ∑w^(*n*)\=1/(1−w), differentiating the last expression with respect to w gives the following: Sum ∑n w^(*n*−1)\=1/(1− w)² or sum ∑(n + 1) w^(*n*)\=1/(1−w)². Now substituting in for w gives ∑ \[1/*π* (n + 1) z^(*n*)\* u^(*n*)\]=1/(1−z\* u)².#

 

### Example 19.4

The Mittag-Leffler real-valued RKHS of order q> 0 consists of functions in $F = \\left\\{ f\\left( z \\right) = \\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}{a\_{n} z^{qn}} \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000278si121.png), such that $\\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}\\left. {|a\_{n}|}^{2}\\Gamma\\left( {{qn} + 1} \\right) < \\infty \\right\\}$![Equation](Images/F000278si122.png), where the gamma function is *Γ*(*z*) = ∫[0]^∞*t*^(*z* − 1)*e*^( − *t*)*d**t*![Equation](Images/F000278si123.png). The kernel is given by the Mittag-Leffler function: *K*[*q*](*λ*, *t*) = *E*[*q*](*λ*^(*q*), *t*^(*q*))![Equation](Images/F000278si124.png), where $E\_{q}\\left( z \\right) = \\overset{\\infty}{\\underset{n = 0}{\\sum^{}}}z^{n}/{\\lbrack{\\Gamma{({{qn} + 1})}}\\rbrack}$![Equation](Images/F000278si125.png). This function is entire and generalizes the exponential function. When q=1, *E*[1](*z*) = *e*^(*z*)![Equation](Images/F000278si126.png); moreover, when the Bargmann-Fock space is restricted to the positive x-axis, the Mittag-Leffler real-valued RKHS is a consequence. On the other hand, a complexification of the Mittag-Leffler real-valued RKHS will yield a Mittag-Leffler space of entire functions generalizing the Bargmann-Fock space ([Rosenfeld et al., 2018](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib10)).#

 

### Example 19.5

The Drury-Arveson space is *H*[*n*]²![Equation](Images/F000278si127.png), with B the open unit ball in *C*^(*n*)![Equation](Images/F000278si128.png) for n larger or equal to two. When n=2, this space is a Hilbert space of analytic functions on B with a reproducing kernel K[*Z*](w)=1/(1−<z, w>). It is a RKHS with inner product $< f,g > = {\\sum\\limits\_{ainZ\_{+}^{n}}{\\left( {a!/{|a|}!} \\right)b\_{a}c\_{a}}}$![Equation](Images/F000278si129.png),\* where $f\\left( z \\right) = \\underset{ainZ\_{+}^{n}}{\\sum^{}}b\_{a}z^{a},g\\left( z \\right) = \\underset{ainZ\_{+}^{n}}{\\sum^{}}c\_{a}z^{a}$![Equation](Images/F000278si130.png). This is a generalization of the Hardy RKHS ([Jury and Martin, 2018](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib6)).#

 

### Example 19.6

The Bargmann-Fock space is a RKHS of entire functions F, in the Hilbert space *L*²![Equation](Images/F000278si131.png), with Gaussian measure, namely the inner product in *C*^(*n*)![Equation](Images/F000278si132.png) is given by  < *f*, *g* >  = *π*^( − *n*)∫*f*(*z*) \* *g*(*z*)*e*^(( − *|**z*|²))*d**z*![Equation](Images/F000278si133.png). Specifically, $F = \\left\\{ f\\left( z \\right) = \\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}{a\_{n}z^{n}} \\right.$![Equation](Images/F000278si134.png), such that $\\sum\_{n = 0}^{\\infty}\\left. {|a\_{n}|}^{2}n! < \\infty \\right\\}$![Equation](Images/F000278si135.png). The reproducing kernel is *K*(*z*,*w*) = *e*^(*w**z*\*)![Equation](Images/F000278si136.png), and therefore, *π*^( − *n*)∫^()*e*^(*w**z*\*)*g*(*z*)*e*^(( − |*z*|²))*d**z* = *g*(*w*)![Equation](Images/F000278si137.png) ([Hall, 2013](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib5); [Barbier, 2013](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib2)).#

In the second reference mentioned above, Jordan algebras are used in exploring Fock space as well as Bargmann transforms. In that reference, the algebra involved real-valued symmetric matrices. It is interesting to mention that in the present text, in Example 3.3), a Jordan-type algebra results. This occurs when the subalgebra of real-valued symmetric matrices is employed in that example. In general, a Jordan algebra is a unital, commutative, and usually nonassociative algebra obeying an additional constraint, besides those MSA identities provided in [Section 3.1.](#Ch003_41-55_B9780443136979000175.xhtml#s0010) This equational constraint involves multiplication using BINE or·. It is given by

Jordan identity: BINE (u, BINE (BINE (u, u), v))=BINE (BINE (u, u), BINE (u, v)).

Again, the Jordan identity: u·(u²·v)=u²·(u·v). The more succinct notation may be more understandable. The constraint is a sort of associative type law.

 

### Example 19.7

With the remarks given earlier, consider the carrier set J, of all 2 by 2 real-valued symmetric matrices, u and v. Using BINE (u, v)=(u v + v u)/2, as in Example 3.3), then by substitution, not only is this structure a unital, commutative, nonassociative algebra, but it is also a Jordan algebra.#

## 19.3 Reproducing kernel Hilbert space over R

The function k: X x X→R is a kernel iff there exists a Hilbert space H and a map Φ: X→H such that <Φ(x), Φ(y)>. Given are X and a kernel function, a scalar product, and a mapping Φ: X→H such that k(x,y)=<Φ(x), Φ(y)>. To see this, given X and k there exists a mapping, Φ: X→H where k(x,y)=<Φ(x), Φ(y)>. This exists for all x and y in X. The RKHS is a space of functions. For any x in X, use k[*x*]\=Φ(x)=k(x,·), where we use x as a parameter, and let k[*x*]: X→R, so k[*x*] is a functional. However, every point in X gets mapped into a function. Let S be the range or image of {k[*x*], such that x is in X}. Take the set of all linear combinations, that is, the span of these functions makes S become a vector space. Define the inner product <k*x*, k[*y*]\>=<k(x,·), k(y,·)>=k(x, y). This inner product can be extended for arbitrary functions f and g, where f=$\\sum\\limits\_{i}$![Equation](Images/F000278si139.png) a[*i*] k(x[*i*],·) and g=$\\sum\\limits\_{j}$![Equation](Images/F000278si140.png) b[*j*] k(y[*j*],·). Here, $< f,g > = \\underset{i,j}{\\sum^{}}a\_{i}b\_{j}k{({x\_{i},y\_{j},})}$![Equation](Images/F000278si141.png), and let S′ be the resulting inner product space. If the completion is performed making every Cauchy sequence converge by adding limit points, a RKHS H is obtained.

The kernel is self-reproducing and positive semidefinite. Use <K(., x), K(., y)>=K(y, x)=<K(., y), K(., x)>\*. Thus for the real case, the kernel is symmetric.

 

### Example 19.9

One of the simplest examples of a RKHS is *l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si142.png). Here, these are all functions from the positive integers N into the reals and are square summable. These functions form a vector space and a Hilbert space with induced norm squared ∥*f*∥² = ∑|*f*(*n*)|²![Equation](Images/F000278si143.png). An evaluation functional *E*[*n*] : *l*²→*R*![Equation](Images/F000278si144.png), for each n in N, is *E*[*n*](*f*) = *f*(*n*) =  < *f*, *e*[*n*]\>![Equation](Images/F000278si145.png), where *e*[*n*]![Equation](Images/F000278si146.png) in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si147.png) is such that *e*[*n*](*n*) = 1![Equation](Images/F000278si148.png), and for all other values in N, *e*[*n*](*m*) = 0![Equation](Images/F000278si149.png). Moreover, |*E*[*n*](*f*)|![Equation](Images/F000278si150.png) is less than or equal to ‖f‖, so it is a bounded functional. As an instance, let f (n)=1/n; then f is in *l*²![Equation](Images/F000278si151.png). As an evaluation functional, notice that *E*[3]\=1/3,*a**n**d*∥f∥ = *π*/6^(1/2)![Equation](Images/F000278si152.png).#

 

### Example 19.10

Consider the vector space of affine functions f(t)=a + bt, where a and b are in R. Use the inner product in L²(0, 1), that is, <f, g>=∫[0]¹*f*![Equation](Images/F000278si153.png) g. Then to find the kernel, K(t,s), which recreates the affine function, that is, a + bt=∫[0]¹![Equation](Images/F000278si154.png) (a + b s) K(t,s) ds, first use 1 = ∫[0]¹*K*(*t*,*s*)![Equation](Images/F000278si155.png) ds, and next use *t* = ∫[0]¹*s*![Equation](Images/F000278si156.png) K(t,s) ds. Substituting into the last two equations K(t,s)=a(t) + b(t) s gives 1=a(t) + b(t)/2 and t=a(t)/2 + b(t)/3. Solving for a(t) and b(t) gives 1–2 t=−b(t)/6, so b(t)= −6 +12t and a(t)=4–6t. The kernel is K(t,s)=4–6 (s + t) +12st. To verify the result, note that ∫[0]¹![Equation](Images/F000278si157.png) (a + b s) K(t,s) ds.=4a −3a −6at + 6at +2b −2b −3bt +4bt=a + bt.#

 

### Example 19.11

Consider band-limited functions f(t) in *L*²![Equation](Images/F000278si158.png) that have a Fourier transform *F*(*w*) = ∫^()[ − ∞]^∞*f*(*t*)*e*^( − *i**w**t*)*d**t*![Equation](Images/F000278si159.png), of compact support, on \[−a, a\], a> 0. Because F(w) is also in *L*²![Equation](Images/F000278si160.png) and it is of finite support, then F(w) is also in *L*¹![Equation](Images/F000278si161.png). Consequently f(t) has numerous properties; see the excellent reference ([Goldberg, 1961](#Ch019_349-364_B9780443136979000278.xhtml#bib4)):

1.  1) Inverse Fourier transform: *f*(*t*) = 1/(2*π*)∫^()[ − ∞]^∞*F*(*w*)*e*^(*i**w**t*)*d**w* = 1/(2*π*)∫^()[ − *a*]^(*a*)*F*(*w*)*e*^(*i**w**t*)*d**w*![Equation](Images/F000278si162.png)
